Evolutionary Patterns in Plant NLR Immune Receptor Structure and Function

PhD thesis by AmirAli Toghani, submitted to the University of East Anglia and carried out at The Sainsbury Laboratory, Norwich, September 2026.

8 chapters·66 figures·287 references·53,800 words·163 min read

Abstract

Plant nucleotide-binding leucine-rich repeat (NLR) immune receptors detect pathogen effectors in the cell and trigger immune responses that lead to cell death. Within the superasterid NRC (NLR Required for Cell death) network, sensor NLRs detect pathogens but need NRC helpers to mediate immune signaling and confer disease resistance. NLR evolution has been extensively studied in the context of co-evolution with pathogen effector. However, the degree to which plant NLR evolution is shaped by other selection pressures remains poorly understood.

This thesis studies the relationships between NLRs themselves and the selective pressures that have shaped these NLR–NLR interactions. I investigated the evolutionary dynamics of the NRC network and found that the interfaces mediating helper homodimerization in the resting state have diverged between paralogous clades but remain conserved within lineages. This pattern is consistent with selection acting to keep the signaling pathways of paralogous helpers insulated from one another.

Through comparative evolutionary analysis, I found that sensor NLR diversification rate correlates with helper dependency: sensors dependent on recently derived helpers have diversified more rapidly than those reliant on ancient helpers. These findings indicate that evolutionary pressures beyond direct co-evolution with pathogen effectors act on NLRs to maintain immune network dynamics and robust signaling.

I also showed that AlphaFold 3 can model NLR resistosomes with high confidence and accuracy. The models reproduced experimentally determined structures and resolved the membrane-inserting N-terminal α1 helix, a region frequently missing from cryo-EM structures. Helper NLRs were modeled with higher confidence than their cognate sensors across several sensor–helper systems, including monocot NLR pairs and the NRC network. This supports the hypothesis that sensor NLR subfunctionalization involves loss of the capacity to oligomerize, and provides a structural criterion, complementary to sequence-based methods, for classifying sensor and helper NLRs to help determine genetic dependencies and assist crop breeding.

Chapter 1

General Introduction

10 sections·5 figures·45 min read

Overview

The evolution of plant NLRs is most often interpreted through co-evolution with pathogen effectors. This framework accounts well for how recognition specificities are gained and lost, but it explains considerably less about the remainder of the receptor. The central question of this thesis is therefore what other forces shape NLR sequence and structure. I focus on the following topics: 1. how the evolutionary patterns determine or affect sensor-helper relationships?, 2. how paralogous receptors remain functionally insulated from one another?, and 3. to explore the structural and functional diversity of NLRs using structural modeling. To address these questions, I combined comparative genomics, phylogenomics, and computational structural modeling. I used the superasterids NRC network as the principal system, given its massive but lineage-specific expansion, containing both sensor and helper NLRs, and being well characterized experimentally.

Chapter 1/General Introduction

1.1 An overview of plant immunity

1 min read

Plants are constantly engaged in biotic interactions with their environment, many of which involve pathogenic and parasitic organisms such as fungi, bacteria, oomycetes, and nematodes. To counter these threats, plants have evolved a multi-tiered immune system that protects them against most potential pathogens. This immune system is traditionally conceptualized as two layers of defense. First, upon pathogen contact, plant cell-surface receptors recognize conserved microbe- or pathogen-associated molecular patterns (MAMPs/PAMPs) to mediate an initial defense response named pattern-triggered immunity (PTI). These plasma membrane-associated pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) belong to distinct protein families, most notably leucine-rich repeat receptor-like kinases (LRR-RLKs) and leucine-rich repeat receptor-like proteins (LRR-RLPs) (Dievart et al., 2020; Ngou et al., 2024).

Successful pathogens, however, have evolved to evade or suppress this first line of defense by delivering effector proteins into host cells, leading to effector-triggered susceptibility (ETS) (Ngou et al., 2022). In response, plants evolved intracellular receptors like nucleotide-binding leucine-rich repeat receptors (NLRs) to detect these pathogen-derived effectors (Contreras et al., 2023a). Effector recognition by NLRs activates effector-triggered immunity (ETI), which is often accompanied by a localized form of programmed cell death known as the hypersensitive response (HR) (Jones et al., 2016). NLRs constitute this second layer of plant immunity, and most cloned disease resistance (R) genes in crops belong to this superfamily (Kourelis and Van Der Hoorn, 2018).

Historically, PTI and ETI were viewed as distinct, sequentially acting tiers functioning in a dynamic “zig-zag” model (Jones and Dangl, 2006). Recent studies, however, demonstrate that these two pathways are intimately connected, mutually potentiating one another and sharing overlapping signaling networks (Ngou et al., 2021; Yuan et al., 2021; Pruitt et al., 2021; Tian et al., 2021). In addition, PRRs that cause cell death appear to execute this response via NLRs (Kourelis et al., 2022). In this thesis, I focus primarily on intracellular NLR immune receptors, reviewing our current understanding of their function, structural diversity, and evolution.

1.2 NLR proteins: architecture and function

1 figure·6 min read

1.2.1Domain architecture and the STAND superfamily1.2.2NLRs as molecular switches1.2.3Classes of plant NLRs defined by the N-terminal domain1.2.4Integrated domains and the integrated decoy model

1.2.1 Domain architecture and the STAND superfamily

NLR proteins are found across all kingdoms of life and share a tripartite domain architecture: an N-terminal variable signaling domain, a central nucleotide-binding and oligomerization domain (NOD), and C-terminal superstructure-forming repeats (SSFRs) (Duxbury et al., 2021; Uehling et al., 2017; Dyrka et al., 2020). NLRs belong to the STAND (signal transduction ATPases with numerous domains) superfamily, a distinct lineage of P-loop NTPases that includes key animal and plant regulators of programmed cell death (Leipe et al., 2004). The N-terminal domains typically mediate downstream signaling; in plants, this often culminates in a localized cell death response upon receptor activation (Dyrka et al., 2020; Kourelis et al., 2021). In plant NLRs, the central NOD is specifically an NB-ARC (nucleotide-binding adaptor shared by APAF-1, certain R gene products, and CED-4) domain, while the C-terminal SSFRs are predominantly leucine-rich repeat (LRR) modules (Duxbury et al., 2021; Kourelis et al., 2021).

Although this modular architecture is conserved across kingdoms, the family has diversified far more extensively in plants than in other lineages. Animal NLRs constitute a comparatively small, conserved set of cytosolic sensors that typically assemble into inflammasomes (Duxbury et al., 2021). NLR proteins functioning via analogous signaling logic have also been characterized in fungi and bacteria, where they frequently link to amyloid-forming motifs and cell death-associated domains (Uehling et al., 2017; Dyrka et al., 2020; Daskalov et al., 2016). Plant genomes, by contrast, frequently encode hundreds of diverse NLRs, with repertoire sizes varying by more than an order of magnitude across species (Barragan and Weigel, 2021; Shao et al., 2016; Toghani and Kamoun, 2024; Toghani et al., 2025b; Toghani et al., 2026c). This massive lineage-specific expansion, coupled with high sequence divergence and domain modularity, makes plant NLRs both a compelling model for evolutionary studies and a notoriously difficult target for automated annotation, a challenge addressed in detail in Section 1.8.

1.2.2 NLRs as molecular switches

Like most STAND proteins, plant NLRs function as molecular switches (Takken et al., 2006). In the absence of a pathogen, they are held in an inactive, ADP-bound state, activating immune signaling upon detection of foreign or altered-self elements. The central NB-ARC domain plays a crucial role in this process, facilitating the transition between inactive and active states through the exchange of ADP for ATP (Wang et al., 2019b). While the C-terminal LRR sometimes determines pathogen perception, it also contributes to maintaining the receptor in its inactive state through autoinhibitory interactions. Once the receptor is activated, these inhibitory contacts are released, allowing the N-terminal domain to initiate downstream immune signaling (Förderer et al., 2022; Takken and Goverse, 2012).

The nucleotide-binding pocket that governs this switch is defined by a set of conserved motifs across the NB-ARC domain. These include the P-loop, which coordinates the bound nucleotide, and the MHD motif, which its aspartate makes contacts the ADP β-phosphate in the resting state (Takken et al., 2006; Takken and Goverse, 2012). These motifs have proven both biologically important and experimentally useful. Substitution of the P-loop lysine abolishes nucleotide binding and renders most NLRs inactive, whereas substitution of the MHD aspartate destabilizes the autoinhibited conformation, yielding autoactive receptors that trigger cell death in the absence of pathogen recognition (Wang et al., 2019b; Adachi et al., 2019a). Autoactive MHD mutants are used throughout this thesis to test whether a given receptor is competent to execute cell death independently of upstream activation partners.

1.2.3 Classes of plant NLRs defined by the N-terminal domain

Plant NLRs are classified into distinct groups based on their N-terminal signaling domains, which align with the phylogeny of the NB-ARC domain and point to a deep evolutionary origin for this partitioning. In angiosperms, four main types of N-terminal signaling domains have been described: coiled-coil (CC), RESISTANCE TO POWDERY MILDEW 8 (RPW8)-type (CCR), G10-type CC (CCG10), and Toll/interleukin-1 receptor-type (TIR) (Kourelis et al., 2021). Certain plant lineages like non-flowering plants appear to possess additional types, such as α/β hydrolase and kinase domains (Chia et al., 2022; Andolfo et al., 2019). The N-terminal domain is thought to determine both the nature of the downstream signaling pathway and the specific execution events that follow NLR activation. Throughout this thesis, I refer to CC, CCR, and CCG10 NLRs collectively as CC-type NLRs.

The four classes are unevenly distributed across the plant phylogeny and differ in their functional roles. CC-NLRs are the most phylogenetically widespread and numerically abundant class in angiosperm genomes, comprising both functional singletons and the helper receptors that execute cell death in NLR networks (Shao et al., 2019; Kourelis et al., 2021). TIR-NLRs are abundant in eudicots but have been lost from monocot lineages, with their signaling routed through a dedicated downstream module rather than direct membrane insertion (Lapin et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2023b). CCR-NLRs form a small, highly conserved group that functions almost exclusively as helpers (Saile et al., 2020; Jacob et al., 2021), while CCG10-NLRs are a comparatively poorly characterized class that forms a distinct branch in NB-ARC phylogenies (Kourelis et al., 2021). Because these assignments rest on phylogeny and on the detection of N-terminal domains that are often weakly conserved at sequence level, automated classification can be ambiguous; consequently, a proportion of receptors in any large-scale annotation remain unresolved among the CC-type classes.

1.2.4 Integrated domains and the integrated decoy model

In many plant species, around 3.5% to 10% of NLR proteins deviate from the canonical tripartite architecture by carrying additional integrated domains (IDs), as exemplified by the rice receptors Pik-1 and RGA5 (Cesari et al., 2014; Kroj et al., 2016; Césari et al., 2014). These IDs often resemble host effector targets and play a central role in pathogen detection, either through direct or indirect interactions (Maqbool et al., 2015; Fujisaki et al., 2015; Gu et al., 2023; De La Concepcion et al., 2018). This concept was formalized as the integrated decoy hypothesis, which proposes that plants have genetically incorporated effector targets within NLRs over evolution to detect pathogens and activate host immunity efficiently (Cesari et al., 2014).

Systematic surveys have since shown that the repertoire of integrated domains is broad and evolutionarily labile. Hundreds of distinct domain families have fused to NLRs across the angiosperms, including heavy metal-associated (HMA), WRKY, BED, kinase, and exocyst subunit domains, with identical domain families being integrated independently across divergent lineages (Sarris et al., 2016; Kroj et al., 2016; Marchal et al., 2018; Shao et al., 2024). The presence of an ID is informative regarding both function and recognition mechanism. Because IDs act in perception rather than downstream execution, they are mostly found in sensor NLRs and are typically absent from helpers. Detecting an ID therefore provides one of the few sequence-based criteria available for hypothesizing sensor and helper functions (Białas et al., 2018; Marchal et al., 2018). However, this criterion remains incomplete, as many sensors carry no integrated domain at all. Moreover, it is not clear whether all NLRs with IDs are sensors and rely on other components for signaling. These diagnostic limitations motivate the structural and predictive approaches developed in Chapter 6.

1.3 NLR singletons, pairs, and networks

1 figure·6 min read

1.3.1Functional singletons1.3.2Paired NLRs1.3.3Immune receptor networks1.3.4Modulators and atypical NLRs

1.3.1 Functional singletons

NLRs can function in distinct configurations: as functional singleton NLRs, paired NLRs, or complex NLR networks (Figure 1.2A) (Adachi et al., 2019b; Feehan et al., 2020; Gong et al., 2023). Functional singleton NLRs operate as single genetic units, detecting pathogen effectors and initiating immune signaling without the requirement of additional NLR partners (Adachi et al., 2019b; Adachi et al., 2019a). Well-studied examples include ZAR1 from Arabidopsis thaliana and Sr35 from wheat. ZAR1 does not recognize pathogen effectors directly; instead, it detects them indirectly through its associated receptor-like cytoplasmic kinases (RLCKs), which act as guardees or decoys (Wang et al., 2019a; Adachi et al., 2023b). In contrast, Sr35 binds its cognate effector AvrSr35 directly via its LRR domain (Förderer et al., 2022). Additional NLRs, such as Sr50 (Chen et al., 2017), various members of the barley MLA allelic series (Brabham et al., 2024; Maekawa et al., 2019; Saur et al., 2019; Gómez De La Cruz et al., 2026), and RPS5 (Qi et al., 2012; Pottinger and Innes, 2020), are likewise considered singletons based on their ability to sense effectors and trigger hypersensitive cell death across diverse plant species.

A widely used method to characterize these NLRs is agroinfiltration, in which immune receptors are transiently expressed in the leaves of Nicotiana benthamiana or other amenable plant species to assess their function (Derevnina et al., 2019). This assay is particularly valuable for testing whether an NLR from another plant species can autonomously trigger cell death in N. benthamiana (Derevnina et al., 2019), which provides initial evidence for singleton or helper activity. However, this assay is not definitive on its own, as the outcome depends on the conservation of downstream signaling partners as well as adequate expression and correct subcellular localization. A receptor that fails to induce cell death in this heterologous system may be a dedicated sensor lacking its partner helper, a helper whose downstream components have diverged, or simply a poorly expressed protein. For this reason, the assay is most informative when combined with “autoactive” MHD mutants to test intrinsic cell death execution, and especially when performed in genetic backgrounds where candidate downstream potential helpers have been knocked out.

1.3.2 Paired NLRs

Paired NLR systems operate through division of labor, comprising a sensor NLR dedicated to effector detection and a helper NLR that executes downstream immune signaling. Notable examples of paired NLRs include the rice NLR pairs Pik-1/Pik-2 and RGA5/RGA4 (Maqbool et al., 2015; Gong et al., 2023; Zdrzałek et al., 2020; De La Concepcion et al., 2021), alongside the Arabidopsis TIR-NLR pair RPS4/RRS1 (Sarris et al., 2015; Saucet et al., 2015). In these systems, pathogen recognition by the sensor NLR is communicated to the helper NLR, which then activates immune responses.

The two genes in a pair are typically encoded adjacent to each other in a head-to-head orientation, sharing a common promoter region, with the sensor frequently carrying an integrated domain (Kroj et al., 2016; Sarris et al., 2016). The regulatory mechanism transmitting signals between them varies across pairs. In the RGA5/RGA4 pair, the helper RGA4 is constitutively active and held in an autoinhibited state by the sensor RGA5, such that effector binding relieves negative regulation (Césari et al., 2014). For Pikp-1/Pikp-2, by contrast, the evidence supports cooperative activation of the helper by the sensor upon effector binding (Zdrzałek et al., 2020; Dong et al., 2018; Pai et al., 2025a). Because paired receptors often originate from distinct phylogenetic clades while functioning as a unit, they are more difficult to classify on purely phylogenetic criteria than the known NLR networks, making the identification of sensor and helper partners in candidate pairs a persistent challenge (Kourelis et al., 2021; Contreras et al., 2023a).

1.3.3 Immune receptor networks

Plant NLRs can also organize into interconnected networks that extend beyond isolated sensor–helper pairs (Adachi et al., 2019b; Wu et al., 2018). These networks encompass multiple, often genetically unlinked NLRs, featuring flexible architectures with “one-to-many” or “many-to-one” connections. Multiple sensor NLRs can converge onto a single downstream helper, while individual sensors may also signal through multiple helpers. This architecture provides evolutionary flexibility and robustness to the plant immune system, with helpers exhibiting functional specialization in sensor compatibility and execution dynamics (Adachi et al., 2019b; Wu et al., 2018).

A prominent example of an NLR network occurs in superasterid plants, where NRCs (NLRs required for cell death) serve as central helper nodes (NRC-H). NRC helpers mediate immune responses against a diverse spectrum of pathogens and pests, including oomycetes, fungi, nematodes, insects, viruses, and bacteria (Wu et al., 2017; Derevnina et al., 2021). The sensors that depend on these helpers (NRC-S) fall into two phylogenetic subtypes. Rx-type NRC-S, which include the potato virus X resistance protein Rx, the pepper bacterial spot resistance protein Bs2, and Rpi-amr3, retain the canonical tripartite NLR architecture with occasional integration of IDs in their scaffold (Contreras et al., 2022; Ahn et al., 2023; Lin et al., 2021). The second subclass, named SD-type NRC-S such as Prf, Sw5-b, Hero, and Rpi-blb2 typically carry an additional N-terminal extension termed the Solanaceous domain (SD) (Seong et al., 2020; De Oliveira et al., 2016). The function of the SD is not fully resolved, although in the tomato sensor Prf it provides binding sites for the Pto kinase as well as mediating homotypic interactions (Saur et al., 2015). SD-type NRC-S can also carry integrated domains such as HMA IDs in potato R1 clade sensors (Wang et al., 2026).

The network features functional redundancy, as several sensors can signal through more than one helper. While some helpers can act upstream of numerous sensors, others maintain restricted compatibility (Wu et al., 2017; Goh et al., 2024; Lüdke et al., 2025). This redundancy provides an adaptive defense advantage: when a pathogen effector suppresses a specific helper node, sensors capable of signaling through alternative uninhibited helpers preserve immune output (Derevnina et al., 2021). Similarly, in an independent network, the CCR-NLRs NRG1 and ADR1 function as helpers that execute immune responses downstream of small-molecule signals generated by diverse TIR-type sensor NLRs (Castel et al., 2019; Feehan et al., 2023; Qi et al., 2018).

1.3.4 Modulators and atypical NLRs

Beyond standard sensor and helper categories, NLRs can also modulate the activity of other immune receptors. This was first recognized in genetically linked sensor–helper pairs where the sensor suppresses an otherwise autoactive helper, as seen with RGA5/RGA4. More recent studies have identified atypical NLRs that function as dedicated modulators of immune signaling outside of canonical sensor or helper roles (Cesari et al., 2014; Ma et al., 2018).

NRCX, a full-length CC-NLR closely related to the helpers NRC2 and NRC3, is a representative example. Its N-terminal MADA motif is non-functional, and silencing NRCX in N. benthamiana triggers spontaneous autoimmunity that depends specifically on NRC2 and NRC3, but not NRC4. NRCX therefore acts as a negative regulator of NRC2 and NRC3, likely having evolved to prevent inappropriate activation of these helper pathways in the absence of pathogens (Adachi et al., 2023a). NRCX highlights how atypical NLRs can act as network modulators (Adachi et al., 2023a; Wu et al., 2022). Another example is truncated NLR variants such as NRG1C, which antagonizes immunity mediated by its full-length counterparts NRG1A and NRG1B (Wu et al., 2022). The existence of such modulators indicates that complex network configurations evolved regulatory mechanisms to balance immune output and prevent autoimmunity.

The known network configurations are non-randomly distributed across the plant NLR phylogeny. Within a given network, NRC-S and NRC-H belong to distinct, monophyletic clades. In the superasterids, the NRC superclade, comprising the NRC-H alongside their dependent Rx-type and SD-type NRC-S, forms a well-supported lineage nested within the broader CC-NLR clade (Figure 1.2B).

Chapter 1/General Introduction

1.4 The N-terminal α1 helix and the MADA motif

1 figure·2 min read

The MADA motif, located in the N-terminal α1 helix of about 20% of all angiosperm CC-NLRs, is required for the induction of cell death (Adachi et al., 2019a). This motif, along with related sequences such as the MAEPL motif found in non-flowering plants, is functionally conserved across a wide range of evolutionarily distant NLRs capable of triggering cell death (Chia et al., 2022; Chia and Carella, 2023). NLRs carrying an N-terminal MADA motif include diverse receptors, from the ancient singleton ZAR1 to helper NLRs like Pik-2 and NRC4 (Adachi et al., 2019a). This points to a shared origin for these CC-NLRs and implies that the MADA-type α1 helix has been a feature of the family since the emergence of land plants. However, as sensor NLRs specialized in detecting pathogens, they appear to have frequently lost or degenerated their MADA motif, rendering them unable to initiate immunity independently (Adachi et al., 2019a).

For instance, while NRC helpers carry a MADA motif, the NRC-S that depend on them lack it. Moreover, the N-termini of NLRs containing MADA or MAEPL motifs can functionally replace the N-terminus of the helper NRC4, whereas the N-termini of sensor CC-NLRs cannot (Chia et al., 2022; Adachi et al., 2019a). These observations are consistent with an evolutionary “use-it-or-lose-it” model. Under this model, as sensor NLRs came to rely on helpers for executing cell death, the conserved motifs in their N-termini degenerated into sequences that no longer function for independently activating immunity or causing cell death.

The functional interchangeability of the motif also makes it a useful diagnostic. Because the MADA motif is largely confined to receptors that execute cell death, its presence has been used as a sequence-based criterion to identify candidate helpers and singletons in genomes where functional data are lacking (Adachi et al., 2019a; Kourelis et al., 2021). Like the integrated domain criterion discussed above. However, this more complicated as: 1/ the motif is detected in only around a fifth of CC-NLRs and many non-MADA are capable to cause cell death, 2/ its degeneration in sensors is gradual rather than absolute, and 3/ receptors carrying an apparently intact motif are not always competent to induce cell death.

1.5 Mechanisms of NLR activation

1 figure·10 min read

1.5.1The ZAR1 resistosome and the pentameric paradigm1.5.2Sr35: the second pentameric resistosome1.5.3Activation in the NRC network1.5.4CCG10-NLRs and the octameric resistosome1.5.5TIR-NLR and CCR-NLR signaling

1.5.1 The ZAR1 resistosome and the pentameric paradigm

Recent studies have provided substantial insight into the activation mechanisms of CC-NLRs and of TIR-NLR/CCR-NLR pathways (Wang et al., 2019b; Förderer et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2019a; Ma et al., 2020; Martin et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2022). In functionally singleton CC-NLRs such as Arabidopsis thanliana ZAR1, pathogen detection triggers a cascade of conformational changes leading to the assembly of a wheel-shaped pentameric complex termed the “resistosome”. This activation is driven primarily by the NB-ARC domain: uridylylation of the receptor-like cytoplasmic kinase PBL2 by the bacterial effector AvrAC is sensed through the partner pseudokinase RKS1, which primes the ADP-bound ZAR1 monomer for nucleotide exchange and subsequent oligomerization (Wang et al., 2019b; Wang et al., 2019a).

The resulting pentamer inserts into the plasma membrane through its N-terminal CC domain. In this assembly, the α1 helices of the five protomers, which are buried against the NB-ARC domain in the resting state, swing outward to form a funnel-shaped pore (Wang et al., 2019a). This funnel structure is required for cell death, and electrophysiological studies established that the ZAR1 resistosome acts as a calcium-permeable cation channel, placing sustained calcium influx upstream of the cell death response (Bi et al., 2021). The structure provided a mechanistic model for how effector recognition at the C-terminal LRR is converted into a membrane-associated signaling event at the N-terminus, becoming the reference paradigm against which subsequent CC-NLR assemblies were compared.

1.5.2 Sr35: the second pentameric resistosome

The mechanism first observed for ZAR1 has since been validated in other CC-NLRs. The wheat receptor Sr35 differs from ZAR1 in that it recognizes its cognate effector, AvrSr35, directly through its LRR domain rather than by guarding a host component. Despite this difference, Sr35 also assembles into a pentameric resistosome with the same overall wheel-shaped architecture and comparable calcium channel activity (Förderer et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2022). Two receptors from distantly related plant lineages, using different recognition strategies, thus converge on the same activated architecture. This was taken as evidence for a shared activation pathway, temporarily establishing the pentamer as the canonical active state for CC-NLRs (Förderer et al., 2022).

1.5.3 Activation in the NRC network

In the NRC network the sensor–helper communication and activation mechanism differs substantially from the singleton model. NRC-S trigger the activation and subsequent oligomerization of their downstream helper NRCs without forming a stable complex with them (Contreras et al., 2022; Ahn et al., 2023). The absence of a detectable sensor–helper complex, combined with the observation that activated helpers oligomerize while their upstream NRC-S remain monomeric, is most consistent with a transient “activation-and-release” interaction rather than a persistent heterooligomeric signaling complex (Contreras et al., 2022; Ahn et al., 2023). Further work mapped this activity to the nucleotide-binding domain (NBD) of the sensor NLR, which is sufficient as a minimal unit to trigger helper activation and oligomerization (Contreras et al., 2023c). More recently, we identified the interfaces mediating this transient interaction (Toghani et al., 2026a). Using AlphaFold 3, we could predict a high-confidence model of the sensor NLR Rx in complex with its helper NRC2. We then validated the predicted contacts through loss- and gain-of-function mutagenesis (Toghani et al., 2026a). These sensor–helper interfaces are conserved across asterid NRC networks despite more than 120 million years of divergence. Notably, structure-guided mutagenesis of a lettuce sensor NLR was sufficient to expand the range of its helper compatibility (Toghani et al., 2026a). Together, these findings support the activation-and-release model and show that sensor–helper compatibility is determined by a small number of key contact interfaces.

The resting and activated states of the helper NLRs themselves also diverge from the known singleton model. NRC helpers such as NRC2 exist natively as homodimers rather than monomers (Selvaraj et al., 2024), meaning that upstream sensors must interact and convert a resting homodimer into a higher-order assembly rather than simply activating an autoinhibited monomer. Furthermore, activated NRC2, NRC3, and NRC4 assemble into hexameric resistosomes, deviating from the pentameric structures observed for singletons (Liu et al., 2023a; Madhuprakash et al., 2024; Seager et al., 2026). Remarkably, recently we have also shown that NRC7 from several Solanaceae species assembles into an 11-mer resistosome structure upon activation (Toghani et al., 2026b), suggesting structural and oligomeric diversity even within the same closely related protein family. However, so far, no empirical structure of resting-state or activated NRC-S has been reported. Together, these findings highlight fundamental differences in the resting architecture and activation dynamics of the NRC network relative to singleton CC-NLRs, pointing to potential structural diversity within the NLR family.

1.5.4 CCG10-NLRs and the octameric resistosome

The CCG10-NLRs form a phylogenetically distinct clade within the CC-type NLRs, resolved as a separate lineage in NB-ARC phylogenies of angiosperm receptors and classified as one of the four main N-terminal classes in current plant NLR nomenclature (Shao et al., 2016; Kourelis et al., 2021). This class has remained comparatively understudied despite containing several classic resistance genes, including Arabidopsis RPS2 and RPS5 (Bent et al., 1994; Mindrinos et al., 1994; Qi et al., 2012; Pottinger and Innes, 2020), pepper Pvr4 (Kim et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2023), and soybean Rsv3 (Tran et al., 2018). Functionally, characterized CCG10-NLRs behave like singletons. A genome-wide screen of pepper NLRs identified a group of ancient and autonomous NLRs (ANLs) carrying autoactive coiled-coil domains whose cell death activity requires neither NRCs nor the NRG1/ADR1 helper families, and which localize directly to the plasma membrane like ZAR1 (Lee et al., 2021). Conserved across seed plants, the CCG10 class represents an ancient family that is distinct from both canonical singleton CC-NLRs and the networked helpers discussed above.

This class is further distinguished by sequence divergence in its CC domain. Canonical CC-NLRs carry a conserved EDVID motif in the α3 helix that packs against the NB-ARC domain to support autoinhibition and oligomerization. The sequence variation of this motif tracks structural and functional divergence closely enough that its presence has been proposed as a predictor of canonical resistosome assembly (Sulkowski et al., 2025). CCG10-NLRs lack this EDVID motif, nor do they carry an N-terminal MADA motif. In the case of pepper CCG10-NLRs, cell death activity depends on the structural integrity of the α1 helix itself (Lee et al., 2021; Lee et al., 2023). These features indicated that the N-terminal architecture of CCG10-NLRs diverges significantly from the canonical CC-NLR models, hinting at potential differences in structural configurations in this class.

This hypothesis has recently been confirmed experimentally. Cryo-EM analysis of an activated wheat CCG10-NLR named Wheat AutoImmunity 3 (WAI3GOF), phylogenetically close to Arabidopsis thaliana RPS2, demonstrated that it assembles into an octameric resistosome; RPS2 was likewise shown to form an octamer, indicating that this stoichiometry is possibly conserved across this clade (Guo et al., 2026). The WAI3 resistosome triggers sustained cytosolic calcium influx via a distinct channel pore shaped by the divergent configuration of its CC domain, an arrangement that may be shared by other plant NLRs lacking the EDVID motif (Guo et al., 2026; Sulkowski et al., 2025). Within the CC-type NLRs alone, known resistosome architectures therefore span pentamers, hexamers, and octamers, and 11-mers.

1.5.5 TIR-NLR and CCR-NLR signaling

Plant TIR domains function as NAD+-cleaving enzymes whose catalytic activity is required for cell death (Wan et al., 2019; Horsefield et al., 2019). This activity is shared with animal SARM1 and a diverse family of prokaryotic TIR proteins involved in antiphage defense, indicating that TIR-based enzymatic signaling is an ancient module recruited independently across the tree of life (Essuman et al., 2022; Shi et al., 2022; Ofir et al., 2021).

Catalysis depends on proximity: cryo-EM structures of the activated ROQ1 and RPP1 resistosomes showed that effector recognition drives assembly into tetramers in which four TIR domains are brought together in an asymmetric arrangement, reconstituting composite NADase active sites so that the activated receptor functions as a holoenzyme (Ma et al., 2020; Martin et al., 2020). Subsequent structural work has extended this model to canonical TIR-NLR activation more broadly (Maruta et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2025). Meanwhile, induced proximity via substrate-driven condensation has emerged as an alternative route to the same activated state for TIR-only proteins, of which Arabidopsis thaliana and other land plants encode a substantial repertoire alongside the full-length TIR-NLRs (Song et al., 2024; Duxbury et al., 2020; Bayless et al., 2025).

What this holoenzyme produces has been resolved only recently, revealing not a single molecule but a family of nucleotide-derived second messengers. Beyond the variant cyclic ADP-riboses first associated with plant TIR activity, two classes of products have been identified as the biologically active signals: the phosphoribosyl adenosines pRib-AMP and pRib-ADP (Huang et al., 2022), and the ADP-ribosylated nucleotides ADPr-ATP and di-ADPR (Jia et al., 2022). Plant TIR domains have also been reported to act as 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP synthetases (Yu et al., 2022). The product spectrum differs systematically between plant and prokaryotic TIR domains, with prokaryotes generating distinct cyclic ADPR isomers and, in some bacteria, histidine-ADPR (Bayless et al., 2023; Sabonis et al., 2025; Jia et al., 2023). The signal generated by a TIR-NLR is therefore diffusible and chemically specific, rather than being tied to the membrane insertion of the receptor itself.

These molecules are perceived by the EDS1 signaling hub, which operates as two heterodimeric modules, EDS1–PAD4 and EDS1–SAG101, that act downstream with the helper CCR-NLRs ADR1 and NRG1, respectively (Pruitt et al., 2021; Lapin et al., 2019; Gantner et al., 2019). The second messengers bind an allosteric pocket at the heterodimer interface to promote association with the cognate helper: pRib-AMP/ADP acts on EDS1–PAD4–ADR1, while ADPr-ATP/di-ADPR acts on EDS1–SAG101–NRG1 (Huang et al., 2022; Jia et al., 2022). This mechanism provides a biochemical basis for the effector-dependent recruitment of NRG1 to EDS1–SAG101 observed in planta (Sun et al., 2021).

Specificity between the two branches is determined in part by cavity-lining residues in PAD4 and SAG101 (Dongus et al., 2022). The two branches are also functionally specialized: NRG1 is required primarily for the execution of cell death (Castel et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2019), whereas ADR1 contributes mainly to transcriptional defense reprogramming and the potentiation of pattern-triggered immunity (Saile et al., 2020; Pruitt et al., 2021). The EDS1 family and RNL helpers have coevolved as a functional module and are frequently lost together in lineages lacking TIR-NLRs, notably in monocots, pointing to a tightly constrained signaling unit (Lapin et al., 2020; Baggs et al., 2020; Tarr and Alexander, 2009). Recent work nonetheless indicates that the EDS1–PAD4–ADR1 node itself is conserved and functional in monocots as well as eudicots (Maruta et al., 2025). As in the NRC network, this pathway carries its own endogenous modulators, including the N-terminally truncated variant NRG1C, which antagonizes immunity mediated by full-length NRG1 helpers in Arabidopsis thaliana (Wu et al., 2022).

Despite the divergence in upstream signaling chemistry, the endpoint of both CC-NLR and TIR-NLR pathways converges. Helper CCR-NLRs oligomerize upon activation and associate with the plasma membrane in a manner reminiscent of CC-NLR resistosomes (Feehan et al., 2023; Jacob et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2023). Helper RNLs are activated directly by both plant and bacterial TIR-derived small molecules to assemble into resistosome-like complexes (Yu et al., 2024; Ge et al., 2026). Calcium influx appears to be the shared output: RNL and CC-NLR resistosomes alike act as calcium-permeable channels, and calcium mobilized from both organellar and extracellular pools converges on the execution of cell death (Bi et al., 2021; Bi and Zhou, 2021; Ibrahim et al., 2026; Shen et al., 2024). However, it was recently shown NRG1-type helper NLRs localize to organellar membrane and channel internal calcium deposits from such as chloroplast to induce the calcium influx (Ibrahim et al., 2026), contrasting the known plasma membrane localization of CC-NLR resistosomes. Nevertheless, two receptor classes with entirely different recognition strategies and signaling mechanisms therefore converge on the same execution step, reinforcing the principle that oligomerization into a defined higher-order assembly is the universal mechanism of NLR activation (Hu and Chai, 2023; Wu, 2025).

Chapter 1/General Introduction

1.6 Oligomerization and cell death across the domains of life

1 figure·5 min read

1.6.1Nucleotide-dependent oligomerization as a shared signaling principle1.6.2Executing cell death: convergent routes to membrane permeabilization

1.6.1 Nucleotide-dependent oligomerization as a shared signaling principle

Plant NLRs represent one branch of the STAND clade of P-loop NTPases, a group defined by shared domain architecture and nucleotide-binding chemistry that also encompasses animal NOD-like receptors, the apoptotic regulators APAF-1 and CED-4, and, more distantly, the AAA+ ATPases (Leipe et al., 2004; Duxbury et al., 2021; Seraphim and Houry, 2020; Khan et al., 2022). What these proteins share is not sequence similarity across their peripheral domains, but a common signaling logic: a central nucleotide-binding module acts as a conformational switch, with activation transduced by converting an autoinhibited monomer, or an autoinhibited higher-order assembly, into a defined oligomer that serves as a platform for downstream effector recruitment or activation (Hu and Chai, 2023; Saur et al., 2021).

The apoptosome illustrates this principle in its simplest form, where APAF-1 assembles upon cytochrome c binding into a wheel-shaped heptamer that recruits and activates initiator caspases (Yuan et al., 2013; Pang et al., 2015). The inflammasomes of animal innate immunity, originally described as molecular platforms for activating inflammatory caspases (Martinon et al., 2002), follow an analogous scheme toward different outputs, whether through templated self-propagation of NLRC4 into a disc (Hu et al., 2015), the cage-to-disc transition of NLRP3 (Andreeva et al., 2021; Xiao et al., 2023), or the proteasome-dependent release of an active NLRP1 fragment (Barry et al., 2023; Sundaram et al., 2024; Fu et al., 2024).

This principle extends well beyond animals and plants. Fungal NLR proteins have nucleotide-binding scaffolds fused to amyloid signaling motifs, that act as oligomerization templates leading to the conversion of a downstream effector domain into a self-propagating amyloid state, as seen in the HET-s/HET-S incompatibility system and the NWD2 receptor (Uehling et al., 2017; Daskalov et al., 2016; Seuring et al., 2012; Greenwald et al., 2010; Gaspar and Pawlowska, 2022). Similar motifs occur across bacterial genomes (Dyrka et al., 2020). Bacterial NLR proteins have since been shown to function in antiphage defense, representing part of a broader paradigm in which components of eukaryotic cell-autonomous immunity have prokaryotic or archaeal antecedents acquired through horizontal gene transfer and domain shuffling (Kibby et al., 2023; Gao et al., 2022; Aravind et al., 2024; Wein and Sorek, 2022; Bernheim et al., 2024; Culbertson and Levin, 2023; Le ao et al., 2024; Johnson and Kranzusch, 2022).

The NLR family itself is correspondingly ancient within eukaryotes: plant NLRs have been traced to chlorophyte green algae and retain recognizable structural and functional hallmarks across that evolutionary distance (Ortiz and Dodds, 2018; Busche and Laflamme, 2024; Feng et al., 2024), while animal NLRs are already present and diversified in sponges (Yuen et al., 2014). What is conserved across these systems is proximity-driven activation mediated by an oligomerizing scaffold rather than a fixed oligomeric geometry. NLR assemblies range from the heptameric APAF-1 apoptosome to the octameric CED-4 apoptosome (Qi et al., 2010), and from discs and filaments in animal inflammasomes to the tetramers, pentamers, hexamers, octamers, and 11-mers identified in plants. That stoichiometry remains variable even where the overall activation mechanism is conserved is a central theme addressed directly in Chapter 5.

1.6.2 Executing cell death: convergent routes to membrane permeabilization

This evolutionary comparison is informative about how these pathways end as well as how they begin. In animals, both pyroptosis and necroptosis terminate in the permeabilization of the plasma membrane by a dedicated executor protein distinct from the upstream receptor. Inflammasome-activated caspases cleave gasdermins, releasing an N-terminal fragment that oligomerizes within the membrane to form a large β-barrel pore (Ding et al., 2016; Ruan et al., 2018; Broz et al., 2020). Similarly, during necroptosis, RIPK3 phosphorylates the pseudokinase MLKL, which then translocates to the plasma membrane to permeabilize it (Murphy et al., 2013; Petrie et al., 2019; Samson et al., 2020). Both executor classes are ancient: gasdermins occur in fungi and bacteria, where bacterial gasdermin pores function in antiphage defense (Chen and Broz, 2024; Johnson et al., 2024; De Schutter et al., 2021). In animals, sensing and execution are therefore separated across multiple regulatory steps, and the terminal rupture of the membrane is itself a regulated event mediated by NINJ1 (Degen et al., 2023; Newton et al., 2024). These pathways exhibit significant crosstalk, with pore-forming executors recurring widely as the terminal step in regulated cell death (Ai et al., 2024; Snyder and Oberst, 2021; Mesa-Galloso et al., 2021).

In the canonical NLR pathways, singleton and helper NLR resistosome funnel formed by the N-terminal α1 helices inserts directly into the membrane and acts as a calcium-permeable channel. Consequently oligomerization and membrane permeabilization are mediated by a single NLR receptor rather than distributed across an extended protease cascade (Bi et al., 2021; Förderer et al., 2022; Bi and Zhou, 2021).

Even so, these plant and animal systems converge on a shared proximal trigger, as sustained calcium influx precedes cell death in both kingdoms (Bi et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2026). However, more recently some NLRs have been reported to require non-NLR components for immune signaling. Plants encode a family of MLKL-like proteins that function in TIR-NLR immunity and mediate cytoplasmic calcium influx (Mahdi et al., 2020; Shen et al., 2024), and a wheat receptor pair was recently shown to execute cell death through an auxiliary MLKL helper (Bennett et al., 2026). Dedicated executors and self-executing receptors can therefore both operate in plants across distinct signaling branches (Maekawa et al., 2023; Pitsili et al., 2019).

Chapter 1/General Introduction

1.7 The evolution of NLR immune receptors

5 min read

1.7.1The classical view: co-evolution with pathogen effectors1.7.2Emergence of networks from singleton ancestors1.7.3Genomic organization and the mechanics of NLR diversification1.7.4Asymmetric evolution of sensors and helpers1.7.5Evolutionary pressures beyond R–AVR co-evolution

1.7.1 The classical view: co-evolution with pathogen effectors

NLRs are among the most evolutionarily dynamic families of plant proteins and are under constant pressure to evolve (Adachi et al., 2023b; Prigozhin and Krasileva, 2021; Tamborski and Krasileva, 2020). Selection can drive the recognition of new pathogen effectors or host targets, or promote evasion from effector-mediated suppression. The signature of this process is most visible in the LRR, where exposed residues on the concave side show evidence of diversifying selection, both between species and within populations (Prigozhin and Krasileva, 2021; Prigozhin et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2005).

At the repertoire level, NLR gene numbers range from a handful to well over a thousand per genome. They are generally understood to follow a birth-and-death model, in which gene duplication continually generates new receptors, some of which are retained for their recognition capability while others are lost or pseudogenized (Michelmore and Meyers, 1998; Seong et al., 2020; Wingen et al., 2025). As a result, presence/absence variation is common, in a way that a receptor present in one accession of a species may be entirely absent from another (Van De Weyer et al., 2019; Barragan and Weigel, 2021). The forces behind this turnover are not limited to selection for new recognition specificities. Mutation, recombination, and the rates of duplication and deletion all contribute, and population genomics offers a way to weigh their relative contributions across a repertoire rather than one receptor at a time (Wingen et al., 2025). Pathogens add a further layer of pressure by directly targeting immune receptors: the Solanaceae helper NLRs NRC2 and NRC3 are suppressed by the cyst nematode effector SS15 and the oomycete effector AVRcap1b (Derevnina et al., 2021). In some species NRC3 has accumulated substitutions in the effector-binding loop that allow it to evade suppression (Contreras et al., 2023b).

1.7.2 Emergence of networks from singleton ancestors

The evolution of CC-NLRs in plants reflects a transition from an ancestral singleton to complex networks with specialized partners. This shift, driven by the need for rapid adaptation to evolving pathogen effectors, resulted in the formation of dedicated sensor and helper NLRs, each fulfilling distinct roles during the immune response (Wu et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2017). This division of labor is thought to offer several advantages. It alleviates evolutionary constraints on individual NLRs, enabling faster diversification and functional specialization. Sensor NLRs can also more readily incorporate additional domains, such as IDs or the SD, to expand their detection capabilities without being constrained by execution requirements (Cesari et al., 2014; Seong et al., 2020; Białas et al., 2021). This modularity, seen in both paired and networked configurations, is likely a key driver of the adaptability of the plant NLR family.

1.7.3 Genomic organization and the mechanics of NLR diversification

The distribution of NLR genes in plant genomes provides further insight into their evolutionary history. In plants such as Arabidopsis, about half of the NLRs are found in clusters formed through tandem gene duplication or unequal crossing-over events (Lee and Chae, 2020; Van De Weyer et al., 2019). Others are scattered throughout the genome and often lack introns, which suggests expansion via retroduplication (Kim et al., 2017). These duplication processes allow NLRs to develop new functions and domain architectures, leading to diverse gene clusters containing either phylogenetically related genes or a mix of different NLR types (Adachi et al., 2019b).

Sensor–helper NLR pairs, such as the rice pairs Pik-1/Pik-2 and Pia (RGA5/RGA4), are typically found in close genetic proximity, often in head-to-head arrangements (Cesari et al., 2014; Białas et al., 2021; Stein et al., 2018). This close linkage likely facilitates transcriptional co-regulation and ensures that functionally dependent sensor and helper pairs are co-inherited. This is especially important given that some helpers are intrinsically active and could trigger autoimmunity in the absence of their corresponding sensor (De La Concepcion et al., 2018; Ashikawa et al., 2008).

In contrast, the NRC network in asterids shows a different pattern, where NRC-S and NRC-H are mostly genetically dispersed despite their common evolutionary origin (Wu et al., 2017). Within this network, some helper clades can nonetheless remain linked with their cognate NRC-S, as seen for the NRC6 and Hero clades (Lüdke et al., 2023). The ancestral helper NRC0 is likewise found in a conserved cluster with the NRC-S that depend on it (Sakai et al., 2024). Overall, NRC-S and NRC-H belong to distinct but related phylogenetic clades. The network dates back roughly 120 million years and probably evolved from an initial sensor/helper gene pair derived from an ancestral singleton NLR (Goh et al., 2024; Sakai et al., 2024). In the TIR-NLR/CCR-NLR network, helper NLRs like NRG1 and ADR1 and their upstream TIR-NLRs likewise form distinct phylogenetic groups and may have evolved from similar functional pairings (Liu et al., 2023b).

1.7.4 Asymmetric evolution of sensors and helpers

A prediction that follows from this division of labor is that sensors and helpers should experience different selective regimes. Sensors track rapidly evolving effectors and are expected to diversify, whereas helpers are constrained by the need to remain compatible with many upstream partners and are expected to be more conserved. The broad generalization in the literature is indeed that sensors evolve rapidly while helpers remain conserved (Goh et al., 2024). Within the NRC network, NRC0 stands out as the most ancient and conserved helper and is often genetically linked to its dependent sensors, whereas more derived helpers have undergone lineage-specific expansions and occupy varied genomic positions (Goh et al., 2024; Sakai et al., 2024; Lee et al., 2021). A comparable pattern is seen for ZAR1, which has remained atypically conserved across angiosperm evolution while the ZRK guardees on which it depends for recognition have greatly diversified (Adachi et al., 2023b). This generalization, however, is unlikely to be the whole story. Helpers face competing selective demands: they must remain compatible with multiple upstream sensors while also evading effectors that target them directly, two pressures that pull in opposite directions (Derevnina et al., 2021; Contreras et al., 2023b).

1.7.5 Evolutionary pressures beyond R–AVR co-evolution

The selective pressures described so far are most often framed in terms of classic R–AVR co-evolution, and the recognition surfaces of sensor NLRs clearly bear this signature. A substantial part of NLR sequence evolution, however, appears to concern the relationships among NLRs themselves rather than their interactions with pathogens. This includes the requirement that a receptor signal correctly and exclusively to its intended partners, that paralogous nodes remain insulated from one another. Insulation of this kind would preserve functional redundancy, minimize undesired cross-activation between pathways, and provide a route to evade pathogen effectors that suppress individual helpers (Selvaraj et al., 2024; Derevnina et al., 2021; Contreras et al., 2023b). Moreover, the network activity should be kept in check by modulators such as NRCX (Adachi et al., 2023a).

Chapter 1/General Introduction

1.8 Genome-scale resources for studying NLR evolution

4 min read

1.8.1The expansion of sequenced plant genomes1.8.2Why NLRs are particularly affected1.8.3Deep-learning gene annotation

1.8.1 The expansion of sequenced plant genomes

Over the past two decades, the number of publicly available plant genome assemblies has grown from a handful of model species to many hundreds spanning the land plant phylogeny, driven largely by falling sequencing costs and the maturation of long-read technologies (Marks et al., 2021). This rapid accumulation of genomes has opened the door to large-scale comparative analyses of plant gene families, allowing tracing gene gain and loss, copy-number variation, and lineage-specific expansions across broad evolutionary distances. Sampling has also deepened within species, so that many crops are now represented by pangenomes assembled from dozens of accessions rather than by a single reference genome (Zhou et al., 2022; Li et al., 2023; Van Workum et al., 2024). For a gene family as variable as the NLRs, this shift matters, since a single reference genome captures only a fraction of the receptors segregating in a species.

However, the value of such comparisons depends critically on the consistency of the underlying gene annotations. Unlike genome assembly, gene annotation has not been standardized: genomes are annotated with different gene predictors, different sources and depths of transcript or protein evidence, and different parameter choices. This can lead to orthologous sequences to be modeled as a gene in one species but missed entirely in another (Salzberg, 2019). This annotation heterogeneity can systematically bias comparative results. Mixing annotation methods across a clade has been reported to inflate the apparent number of lineage-specific genes by up to 15-fold (Weisman et al., 2022; Van Oss and Carvunis, 2019), whereas errors in gene number inferred from draft assemblies are pervasive (Denton et al., 2014). The same problem confounds presence/absence analyses, where the apparent absence of an ortholog in a heterogeneous dataset may reflect poor or inconsistent annotation rather than true gene loss.

1.8.2 Why NLRs are particularly affected

NLRs are highly diverse and rapidly evolving, which makes them a compelling subject for evolutionary study but also a particularly challenging gene family to annotate consistently (Barragan and Weigel, 2021; Michelmore and Meyers, 1998; Shao et al., 2016; Prigozhin et al., 2025). Their modular, repetitive domain structure, their tendency to occur in dense tandem clusters, and their frequent location in repeat-rich or transposon-rich regions all frustrate standard gene-prediction pipelines. Because of this, often specialized motif-aware tools are required to recover the full repertoire (Steuernagel et al., 2015; Steuernagel et al., 2020; Li et al., 2016; Kourelis et al., 2021; Jupe et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2017).

The consequences are not evenly distributed across the family. Clustered NLRs are prone to being merged into chimeric gene models or split across several partial ones; pseudogenized copies may be annotated as functional or omitted altogether, and receptors carrying integrated domains are especially liable to be truncated at the point of fusion. Because these failure modes is largely dependent on the pipeline, the same locus can be represented quite differently in two genomes annotated by different groups, and comparative counts of NLR repertoire size can reflect annotation practice as much as biology. Curated resources such as NCBI RefSeq provide high-quality, internally consistent annotations, but only for a limited number of reference genomes (Pruitt et al., 2007), which leaves the great majority of published assemblies outside any harmonized standard.

1.8.3 Deep-learning gene annotation

Gene annotation has long relied on ab initio gene finders built on hidden Markov models, an approach pioneered in eukaryotes in part on compact fungal genomes (Ter-Hovhannisyan et al., 2008; Min et al., 2017). These tools remain widely used, but they depend on genome-specific training or on transcript and protein evidence, and their parameters and outputs still vary from assembly to assembly. A more recent generation of deep-learning annotators aims to close this gap by predicting gene models directly from genomic DNA sequence. Helixer, for example, uses a deep neural network to assign each base to a structural category and then resolves these base-wise predictions into gene models with a hidden Markov model (Stiehler et al., 2021). Because a single model is trained once per lineage on curated NCBI RefSeq annotations and then applied uniformly across genomes, such tools can produce internally consistent, harmonized annotations at scale (Stiehler et al., 2021; Holst et al., 2023). The paradigm is developing quickly, with recent tools coupling deep learning to differentiable HMMs and to large DNA foundation models (Gabriel et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025; Vader et al., 2026).

However, no pipeline is perfect. While tools like Helixer are trained on high-quality datasets such as NCBI RefSeq, applying a single model uniformly across genomes harmonizes gene models rather than necessarily improving them. Deep-learning predictors are themselves imperfect and carry their own systematic biases, so a harmonized annotation is best understood as internally consistent rather than error-free (Sugihara et al., 2026). With that qualification, harmonized annotation removes one of the main confounders in comparative analysis of a family as annotation-sensitive as the NLRs.

Chapter 1/General Introduction

1.9 Structural biology and computational modeling of NLRs

4 min read

1.9.1What experimental structures have revealed1.9.2Protein structure prediction and its extension to complexes1.9.3Applications to plant immunity and their limits

1.9.1 What experimental structures have revealed

Over the past few years, a succession of cryo-EM structures has transformed our understanding of NLR-mediated immunity. These resolve several activated receptor complexes, including the ZAR1 and Sr35 pentamers, the tetrameric TIR-NLR resistosomes ROQ1 and RPP1, and most recently, the hexameric NRC2 and NRC4 assemblies alongside the resting-state NRC2 homodimer (Wang et al., 2019a; Förderer et al., 2022; Martin et al., 2020; Ma et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2023a; Madhuprakash et al., 2024; Selvaraj et al., 2024). Collectively, these structures established that NLR activation proceeds through oligomerization, while demonstrating that oligomeric state and signaling output differ systematically across classes.

Despite these advances, each structure required substantial effort in protein purification, sample preparation, and data collection, and as a result coverage remains restricted to a small number of model receptors relative to the size of the family. Moreover, within these structures, the N-terminal α1 helix that forms the CC-type resistosome funnel is structurally dynamic and frequently unresolved or only partially resolved in the resulting maps (Förderer et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2023a; Madhuprakash et al., 2024). Consequently, the region responsible for membrane insertion and cell death execution is missing from experimental data and has remained elusive.

1.9.2 Protein structure prediction and its extension to complexes

Computational structure prediction offers a complementary route. AlphaFold 2 made accurate monomer prediction available (Jumper et al., 2021; Senior et al., 2020), and its multimer extension allowed researchers to model protein complexes (Evans et al., 2021). AlphaFold 3, in addition to faster prediction speed and overall improvements, added the capacity to model proteins together with ligands, ions, and small molecules (Abramson et al., 2024). This feature was proven to be highly relevant for NLR biology, as CC-type NLR resistosomes could be modeled with lipids binding to the N-terminal α1 helix, simulating the plasma membrane.

These tools also report a set of internal confidence metrics that indicate how far a given model should be trusted. The most widely used are the per-residue predicted Local Distance Difference Test (pLDDT), the pairwise Predicted Aligned Error (PAE), and the model-wide predicted template modeling (pTM) and ipTM scores (Jumper et al., 2021; Evans et al., 2021; Abramson et al., 2024). Each captures a different aspect of a prediction and they are most informative when interpreted together, since a complex can score modestly overall while still containing local regions that are modeled with high confidence and are biologically meaningful (Posbeyikian et al., 2026). These metrics also carry known biases. The ipTM score, for instance, is sensitive not only to the size of the interface but also to the total length of the proteins, and it decreases when one partner is disordered even if the interface itself is modeled correctly. Several complementary interface scores have been developed to address this, including ipSAE, pDockQ, and the Local Interaction Score (LIS), which allow predicted complexes to be assessed at scale without manual inspection of PAE plots (Posbeyikian et al., 2026).

Prediction is also a stochastic process. These tools use random seeds to initialize the masking or subsampling of the multiple sequence alignment (MSA), and in the diffusion-based models such as AlphaFold 3 the seed additionally sets the initial noise pattern from which the structure is generated. Because proteins exist as ensembles of related conformations rather than as single static structures, a given run may converge on a local solution. Sampling several seeds and asking whether the same model is recovered each time is therefore a practical way to distinguish robust structural features from stochastic variation (Posbeyikian et al., 2026). The depth of the MSA matters for the same reason: AlphaFold 2 depends heavily on deep evolutionary profiles and tends to struggle with fast-evolving or lineage-specific proteins, whereas AlphaFold 3 relies more on learned structural priors and is comparatively less sensitive to shallow alignments (Posbeyikian et al., 2026). This is directly relevant for NLRs, which are among the most rapidly evolving gene families in plants and frequently return shallow alignments.

1.9.3 Applications to plant immunity and their limits

Structure prediction has already been applied extensively to NLR biology, including structure-informed comparative analyses of receptors and effectors, classification of proteins whose relationships are not resolvable from sequence alone, and modeling-guided engineering of recognition specificity (Ibrahim et al., 2023; Seong and Krasileva, 2021; Barrio-Hernandez et al., 2023; Contreras et al., 2023b).

Because every predicted structure is effectively a hypothesis, benchmarking is the most direct way to decide how far to trust one. Where an experimental structure exists, it should be modeled alongside the targets of interest and used as a reference. Negative controls matter just as much, since confidence scores on their own often cannot separate a genuine complex from a plausible-looking artifact (Posbeyikian et al., 2026).

Low-confidence or unexpected predictions can be informative rather than simply being failures. Interpreted against what is already known about a protein family, they can point to architectures or functions that depart from the canonical model (Posbeyikian et al., 2026). NRC helpers, for example, generally model with high confidence as hexamers. Through a systematic inspection of outliers in a large-scale prediction we found that the NRC7 clade deviates from this arrangement, which was subsequently confirmed as an 11-mer by electron microscopy (Toghani et al., 2026b; Posbeyikian et al., 2026). The same logic applies to the sensor–helper distinction, since sensors typically fail to return confident oligomeric predictions while helpers generally model with higher confidence. This prediction confidence can itself carry functional information to classify NLRs (Toghani et al., 2025a; Pai et al., 2026; Posbeyikian et al., 2026).

However, predictions are therefore best treated as hypotheses to be tested rather than as direct substitutes for experimental structures. Predictions are made in the absence of the cellular context in which these receptors operate, lacking membranes, partners, or post-translational modifications unless these are supplied explicitly. They also depend on the depth and quality of the multiple sequence alignment available for a given receptor, which may vary across the NLR family.

Chapter 1/General Introduction

1.10 Aims and thesis outline

2 min read

The evolution of plant NLRs is most often interpreted through co-evolution with pathogen effectors. This framework accounts well for how recognition specificities are gained and lost, but it explains considerably less about the remainder of the receptor. The central question of this thesis is therefore what other forces shape NLR sequence and structure. I focus on the following topics: 1. how the evolutionary patterns determine or affect sensor-helper relationships?, 2. how paralogous receptors remain functionally insulated from one another?, and 3. to explore the structural and functional diversity of NLRs using structural modeling. To address these questions, I combined comparative genomics, phylogenomics, and computational structural modeling. I used the superasterids NRC network as the principal system, given its massive but lineage-specific expansion, containing both sensor and helper NLRs, and being well characterized experimentally.

In Chapter 2 I establish the resources on which the remainder of the thesis depends on. Because annotation heterogeneity can be mistaken for biological signal in a gene family as variable as the NLRs, I compiled three NLRome datasets at nested taxonomic resolutions and re-annotated the underlying genomes with a single deep-learning pipeline. This allows repertoire size, class composition, and presence or absence of individual clades to be compared across genomes in a harmonized manner.

In Chapter 3 I examine two features of the NRC helper clade that does not directly relate to effector recognition. I first analyze the diversity of the N-terminal MADA motif across the clade, identify a sequence signature shared between the modulator NRCX and a previously undescribed group of NRC4 sequences, and test the functional consequences of that signature in cell death assays. I then turn to the interfaces which NRC2 self-associates in its resting state, and determine whether these have diverged between paralogous helpers in the manner expected if selection acts to keep their signaling pathways insulated from one another.

In Chapter 4 I extend my analysis from individual helpers to entire networks. I compare the architecture and genomic organization of the NRC network between the Asterales and the Solanales, establish experimentally sensor-helper relationships in lettuce, and test whether these relationships shaped the evolution of the network.

In Chapter 5 I address the same problem from a structural perspective. I benchmark AlphaFold 3 against the CC-NLR resistosomes that have been determined experimentally, and then apply the same approach to receptors whose structures remain unsolved, in order to establish how far oligomeric state varies across the CC-type NLRs and whether it can be inferred computationally.

In Chapter 6 I test the extent to which sensors and helpers can be distinguished by their predicted oligomeric structures, evaluate this criterion against the sequence-based ones currently used for the same purpose, and apply it to NLR pairs and networks for which functional data are limited.

Finally, in Chapter 7 I discuss what I learned about the forces acting on immune receptors within a network, and about the extent to which structural prediction can assisst experimental characterization and classification of NLR proteins.

Chapter 2

Curation of harmonized plant NLRome datasets on multiple taxonomic resolutions

5 sections·4 figures·20 min read

Overview

In this chapter I curated three NLR datasets spanning nested taxonomic resolutions, together comprising 756 plant genomes and more than 400,000 cataloged NLRs. The three collections were designed to complement one another: 180 RefSeq reference proteomes provide a broad, uniformly annotated view of NLR diversity across the green plant lineage; 230 superasterid genomes narrow the focus to the phylogenetic distribution of the NRC network while increasing sampling density; and 346 Solanaceae genomes add the depth needed to compare NLR repertoires within, as well as between, species. Except for the RefSeq set, which was already annotated to a consistent standard, all genomes were re-annotated de novo with a single Helixer model and processed through an identical NLRtracker pipeline, so that differences between genomes reflect biology rather than the pipeline-to-pipeline heterogeneity that motivated this work.

About this chapter

The work described in this chapter was carried out in collaboration with Yu Sugihara (The Sainsbury Laboratory). For the superasterid dataset, I collected and compiled the genome assemblies from NCBI Datasets (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/datasets/), and ran the Helixer and NLRtracker pipelines together with Yu Sugihara. For the Solanaceae dataset, Yu Sugihara and I collected the genomes together, and ran the Helixer, NLRtracker, and BUSCO pipelines. All downstream analyses, data curation, and interpretations presented in this thesis were performed by me.
