Chapter 2/Curation of harmonized plant NLRome datasets on multiple taxonomic resolutions

2.1 Introduction

1 figure·6 min read

Over the past two decades, the number of publicly available plant genome assemblies has grown from a handful of model species to many hundreds spanning the land plant phylogeny, driven largely by falling sequencing costs and the maturation of long-read technologies (Marks et al., 2021). This rapid accumulation of genomes has opened the door to large-scale comparative analyses of plant gene families, allowing researchers to trace gene gain and loss, copy-number variation, and lineage-specific expansions across broad evolutionary distances. However, the value of such comparisons depends critically on the consistency of the underlying gene annotations. Unlike genome assembly, gene annotation has not been standardized: genomes are annotated with different gene predictors, different sources and depths of transcript or protein evidence, and different parameter choices, so that orthologous sequences may be modeled as a gene in one species but missed entirely in another (Salzberg, 2019). This annotation heterogeneity can systematically bias comparative results. It has been reported that mixing annotation methods across a clade can inflate the apparent number of lineage-specific genes by up to 15-fold (Weisman et al., 2022; Van Oss and Carvunis, 2019), and errors in gene number inferred from draft assemblies are pervasive, with a majority of genes assigned the wrong copy number in some datasets (Denton et al., 2014). The same problem confounds presence/absence analyses, where the apparent absence of an ortholog or paralog in a heterogeneous dataset may reflect poor or inconsistent annotation rather than true gene loss. Distinguishing biological signal from annotation artifact therefore requires harmonized, high-quality datasets, making the production of consistently annotated genome collections a prerequisite for robust comparative genomics.

In plant immunity, the nucleotide-binding leucine-rich repeat receptor (NLR) family of proteins has been extensively studied due to its crucial role in pathogen recognition and the activation of immune responses (Jones and Dangl, 2006; Jones et al., 2016; Dodds et al., 2024). NLRs are highly diverse in plants and rapidly evolving, which makes them a compelling subject for evolutionary study but also a particularly challenging gene family to annotate consistently (Barragan and Weigel, 2021; Michelmore and Meyers, 1998; Shao et al., 2016; Prigozhin et al., 2025). NLR annotation has historically been difficult: their modular, repetitive domain structure, their tendency to occur in dense tandem clusters, and their frequent location in repeat-rich or transposon-rich regions all frustrate standard gene-prediction pipelines, so that specialized motif-aware tools are typically required to recover the full repertoire (Steuernagel et al., 2015; Steuernagel et al., 2020; Li et al., 2016; Kourelis et al., 2021; Jupe et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2017). As a result, NLR gene models are especially sensitive to how a genome was annotated, and comparative studies of this family depend on high-quality and comparable annotations. Yet among publicly available genomes, many lack author-provided annotations altogether, and where annotations do exist the pipelines and parameter choices used to generate them differ from study to study, which can markedly affect how gene families such as NLRs are resolved (Toghani and Kamoun, 2024; Toghani et al., 2026c; Weisman et al., 2022). Curated resources such as NCBI RefSeq provide high-quality, internally consistent annotations, but only for a limited number of reference genomes (Pruitt et al., 2007).

Gene annotation has long relied on ab initio gene finders built on hidden Markov models. This approach was pioneered in eukaryotes on compact fungal genomes: GeneMark-ES introduced unsupervised self-training of a hidden Markov model (HMM) directly on genomic sequence (Ter-Hovhannisyan et al., 2008), and pipelines such as FunGAP later combined several such predictors with evidence-based model selection to annotate fungal assemblies (Min et al., 2017). These tools remain widely used, but they depend on genome-specific training or on transcript and protein evidence, and their parameters and outputs still vary from assembly to assembly. A more recent generation of deep-learning annotators aims to close this gap by predicting gene models directly from genomic DNA sequence. Helixer, for example, uses a deep neural network to assign each base to a structural category (intergenic, UTR, coding, or intron) and then resolves these base-wise predictions into gene models with an HMM (Stiehler et al., 2021). Because a single model is trained once per lineage and then applied uniformly across genomes, such tools can produce internally consistent, harmonized annotations at scale, sidestepping much of the pipeline-to-pipeline heterogeneity discussed above. Helixer’s models are trained on curated NCBI RefSeq annotations spanning hundreds of high-quality genomes within a clade, so that the network learns a reference-grade representation of gene structure that generalizes to newly sequenced species of the same lineage (Stiehler et al., 2021; Holst et al., 2023). Dedicated pre-trained models have since been released for fungal and invertebrate genomes alongside those for plants and vertebrates (Holst et al., 2023). This paradigm is developing quickly, with recent tools coupling deep learning to HMMs (Gabriel et al., 2024), to large DNA foundation models (Liu et al., 2025), and to lineage-tailored architectures that push accuracy further, including for fungal genomes (Vader et al., 2026). However, applying a single model uniformly across genomes harmonizes gene models rather than necessarily improving them. The aim is to make annotations mutually comparable, not to claim that any individual gene model is more accurate than an author-provided one. Deep-learning predictors are themselves imperfect and carry their own systematic biases, so a harmonized annotation is best understood as internally consistent rather than error-free (Sugihara et al., 2026).

To study NLR diversity and molecular evolution in plants across different evolutionary depths, I compiled three large-scale datasets from public genomes at three distinct taxonomic resolutions. All three were assembled following the same workflow (Figure 2.1), which begins from high-quality public genome assemblies and branches on a single question: whether harmonized, high-quality annotations already exist for the genomes in question. Where they do, as for RefSeq, the existing proteomes can be used directly; where they do not, gene models are generated de novo with Helixer so that the whole collection rests on a common annotation footing. Both branches then converge on NLR annotation with NLRtracker, followed by curation of the resulting NLR set.

The first dataset comprises 180 RefSeq-annotated green plant (Viridiplantae) genomes and takes the first of these branches. Because these assemblies were accompanied by high-quality reference annotations, I ran NLRtracker (Kourelis et al., 2021) directly on their proteomes to annotate protein domains and extract the NLR repertoire (Toghani and Kamoun, 2024). To examine the phylogeny and evolution of the NRC network more closely, I compiled a second dataset of 230 superasterid genomes. Since many of these lacked pre-existing annotations, I annotated the entire set uniformly using the deep-learning-based gene predictor Helixer (Stiehler et al., 2021) to generate harmonized gene models, subsequently extracting the NLRs with NLRtracker (Toghani et al., 2025b). Finally, to resolve the intra- and inter-specific evolution of Solanaceae NLRs, I assembled a third dataset of 346 Solanaceae genomes. As with the superasterid dataset, I generated de novo annotations using Helixer and extracted the corresponding NLRs (Toghani et al., 2026c). In this chapter, I describe each of these NLR datasets in detail, establishing the methodological foundation for the work presented in the subsequent chapters.

Chapter 2OverviewNext 2.2 Functional annotation of 180 RefSeq reference plant proteomes reveals a dataset of 113,684 NLR proteins

Chapter 2/Curation of harmonized plant NLRome datasets on multiple taxonomic resolutions

2.2 Functional annotation of 180 RefSeq reference plant proteomes reveals a dataset of 113,684 NLR proteins

1 figure·3 min read

The first and taxonomically broadest dataset was assembled from the NCBI RefSeq database (Pruitt et al., 2007), which provides curated, internally consistent annotations for a limited set of reference genomes. I selected 180 reference plant (Viridiplantae; up to September 2024) proteomes spanning a wide phylogenetic range, from algae and gymnosperms through early-diverging flowering plants to monocots and dicots, to survey NLR diversity across the green plant lineage on a uniformly annotated foundation. Because these proteomes were already annotated to RefSeq’s reference standard, no de novo gene prediction was required, and I applied NLRtracker (Kourelis et al., 2021) directly to each proteome. NLRtracker integrates InterProScan (Blum et al., 2025) to identify the constituent domains and motifs of NLR proteins and classifies sequences according to the NLR definition established for RefPlantNLR (Kourelis et al., 2021). Where NCBI-provided annotation BUSCO scores were available (156 of the 180 genomes), completeness was uniformly high (median 98.4%; Figure 2.2A), in line with the reference-grade quality expected of RefSeq annotations.

Using this pipeline, 169 of the 180 species contained at least one predicted NLR. All eleven species without a single NLR were chlorophyte green algae. Across the 169 proteomes, NLRtracker cataloged 113,684 NLRs, distributed highly unevenly (Figure 2.2). Per-genome counts ranged from none to 4,155, with a median of 468 and a mean of 632, and NLRs accounted for a median of 1.0% of each proteome (up to 7.7%). Counts varied by two orders of magnitude, from 33 in Cucurbita maxima to 4,155 in Quercus robur, which is consistent with the lineage-specific expansion and contraction thought to characterize this gene family. Proteome size was only weakly associated with NLR count (Pearson r = 0.42; Figure 2.2B), suggesting that repertoire size is not simply a function of overall gene number.

Classifying NLRs by their N-terminal signaling domain recovered a structural breakdown broadly in line with expectations (Figure 2.2D). CC-NLRs were the most abundant class (53,708; 47.2%), followed by TIR-NLRs (27,076; 23.8%) and a smaller set of CCR-NLRs / RPW8-type helper NLRs (1,360; 1.2%). A further 16.6% could not be unambiguously resolved among the CC/CCR/CCG10 types, and 10.8% remained undetermined. Unlike TIR-only proteins, TIR-NLRs were absent from monocots, recapitulating the well-documented loss of the TIR-NLR class in this lineage (Tarr and Alexander, 2009; Shao et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2023b) and suggesting that the dataset recovers established evolutionary patterns.

Beyond NLR extraction, NLRtracker returned functional annotations for the complete proteome of each species, providing a comparative framework for the domain- and motif-level analyses developed in the following chapters. For each proteome, the pipeline produces identifier lists, GFF3 annotations, and FASTA sequences for both NLRs and NLR-associated genes, together with full-length and deduplicated NB-ARC domain sequences, iTOL-ready domain annotation files, a per-sequence domain metadata table, and the raw InterProScan output. The complete dataset, along with a RefSeq species metadata table and a per-genome table of proteome and NLR statistics, is openly available on Zenodo (Toghani and Kamoun, 2024).

Chapter 2/Curation of harmonized plant NLRome datasets on multiple taxonomic resolutions

2.3 Deep-learning-based annotation of 230 superasterid genomes reveals a harmonized dataset of 91,366 NLRs

1 figure·6 min read

The second dataset was assembled to support phylogenetic and evolutionary analysis of the NRC network, and therefore narrows the taxonomic scope to the superasterids while increasing sampling density. I collected 230 high-quality, publicly available superasterid genomes, representing 227 distinct taxa across 59 families and 14 orders. Potato (Solanum tuberosum) is represented by four independent assemblies, while all other taxa are represented by a single genome. In contrast to the RefSeq collection, many of these genomes lacked author-provided annotations, and those that were available had been generated with different pipelines and parameter settings. To eliminate this as a source of variation, I set aside the existing annotations and produced harmonized de novo annotations for the entire set using the deep-learning annotator Helixer v0.3.2 (Stiehler et al., 2021; Holst et al., 2023). This was run with the –lineage land_plant option so that a single land-plant model was applied uniformly across all genomes. This workflow yielded 10,124,265 predicted protein sequences, with a median proteome size of 38,192 (interquartile range 31,628–48,612). Coding sequences and proteomes were extracted from the Helixer GFF output with GffRead v0.12.7 (Pertea and Pertea, 2020), and NLRs and NLR-associated sequences were identified with NLRtracker (Kourelis et al., 2021) using InterProScan for domain assignment (Blum et al., 2025).

Annotation completeness was assessed with BUSCO v5.5.0 against the viridiplantae_odb10 lineage dataset (Manni et al., 2021). The harmonized annotations appeared to be of consistently high quality (Figure 2.3A): BUSCO completeness averaged 95.1% (median 96.7%), with 89.1% of genomes exceeding 90% completeness and 67.0% exceeding 95%. Missing and fragmented BUSCOs were correspondingly low (median 0.7% and 2.4%, respectively). Only five genomes fell below 80% completeness: Striga hermonthica (65.9%), Jacaranda mimosifolia (70.4%), Lactuca virosa (72.9%), Drosera capensis (78.6%), and Artemisia tridentata subsp. tridentata (79.3%). In most of these the deficit was driven by fragmented rather than missing BUSCOs, as in J. mimosifolia (23.1% fragmented versus 6.5% missing) and S. hermonthica (20.2% versus 13.9%), which points to fragmented underlying assemblies rather than a failure of the annotation model; L. virosa was the exception, with 20.0% of BUSCOs missing outright. It is also worth noting that two of these species, the obligate parasite S. hermonthica and the carnivorous D. capensis, have specialized lifestyles associated with genuine gene loss (Li et al., 2025), so reduced BUSCO completeness in such taxa need not reflect annotation quality alone. These five genomes span nearly the full range of NLR content observed across the dataset, from 86 in D. capensis to 1,246 in A. tridentata (Figure 2.3B), and BUSCO completeness showed no correlation with NLR count across the collection as a whole (Pearson r = 0.14). With the exceptions discussed below, this suggests that the variation in NLR repertoire size described later is unlikely to be driven primarily by differences in annotation quality.

Five genomes exceeded 100,000 predicted proteins, and these fall into two apparent classes. In Craterostigma plantagineum (199,483 proteins), 76.9% of BUSCOs were duplicated against only 22.4% single-copy, which most likely reflects genuine retention of homoeologous gene copies in a polyploid genome; the same signature, in milder form, probably explains the elevated duplication seen in Fraxinus americana (98.8% duplicated) and Nicotiana tabacum (94.4%). The remaining cases show the opposite signature: Diospyros kaki (181,147), Dorcoceras hygrometricum (149,066), and Artemisia tridentata subsp. tridentata (132,727) all retain single-copy BUSCO profiles (1.4–1.6% duplicated), so haplotype redundancy is unlikely to account for their inflated gene counts. This is clearest for D. kaki: although the species is an autohexaploid, the assembly used here is a haploid representation, and its single-copy BUSCO profile indicates that retained homoeologs are unlikely to be the source of its 181,147 predicted proteins. Consistent with this, the proteomes obtained for the other two species substantially exceed the published evidence-based annotations for the same genomes: 43,377 genes were reported for A. tridentata (Melton et al., 2022) and 49,374 for D. hygrometricum (Xiao et al., 2015), roughly a third of the counts obtained here. All three are large or difficult to annotate—the A. tridentata assembly is 4.2 Gb and 77.99% repetitive, among the most repetitive plant genomes sequenced to date (Melton et al., 2022), while the D. hygrometricum assembly is an early short-read draft—and both show elevated fragmented BUSCOs (16.5% and 11.3%, respectively). The most likely explanation is therefore over-prediction of gene models in repeat-rich and fragmented sequence, where transposon-derived open reading frames and split loci can be readily called as genes. This failure mode would also be largely invisible to BUSCO, which assays whether a conserved core gene set is present but is insensitive to the addition of spurious models, so high BUSCO completeness should not by itself be read as evidence against over-annotation. NLR counts in these genomes should therefore be interpreted with corresponding caution, particularly for A. tridentata, whose 1,246 NLRs rank among the highest in the dataset.

Applying the NLRtracker definition, this pipeline recovered 91,366 NLRs across the 230 genomes. Per-genome counts spanned more than two orders of magnitude, from 12 to 2,049, with a median of 338 and a mean of 397, and NLRs accounted for a median of 0.80% of each proteome, up to 3.25%. As in the RefSeq dataset, proteome size explained only part of this variation (Pearson r = 0.42). The smallest repertoires belonged to parasitic and carnivorous lineages, namely Cuscuta campestris (12 NLRs), Orobanche coerulescens (19), and Utricularia gibba (32), consistent with the reduced immune receptor repertoires reported for plants with specialized lifestyles and correspondingly altered pathogen exposure (Liu et al., 2021; Baggs et al., 2020). The largest repertoires were found in the Lamiaceae, led by Perilla frutescens (2,049), Pogostemon cablin (1,479), and Thymus mandschuricus (1,466). At the order level, median NLR content varied several-fold, from 82 in Santalales and 167 in Caryophyllales to 401 in Solanales, 582 in Cornales, and 702 in Dipsacales, with the two most densely sampled orders, Lamiales (n = 58) and Solanales (n = 40), showing broad within-order dispersion (Figure 2.3C).

Classifying NLRs by their N-terminal signaling domain gave a breakdown broadly similar to the RefSeq dataset (Figure 2.3D), with CC-NLRs the dominant class (47,276; 51.7%), followed by TIR-NLRs (12,606; 13.8%) and CCR-NLRs / RPW8-type helper NLRs (884; 1.0%). A further 21.1% could not be unambiguously resolved among the CC/CCR/CCG10 types, and 12.0% remained undetermined. The lower TIR-NLR fraction relative to the RefSeq green plant dataset (13.8% versus 23.8%) likely reflects the asterid-focused sampling of this collection.

Genome annotations are organized by phylogenetic order following the APG IV classification (The Angiosperm Phylogeny Group, 2016), with each order held in its own subdirectory containing the genome assembly, GFF annotation, CDS and protein FASTA files, and the corresponding NLRtracker output; compiled proteome and CDS files carrying source-assembly tags are also provided. As for the RefSeq dataset, the NLRtracker output comprises identifier lists, GFF3 annotations, and FASTA sequences for NLRs and NLR-associated genes, full-length and deduplicated NB-ARC domain sequences, iTOL-ready domain annotation files, a per-sequence domain metadata table, and the raw InterProScan output. The complete dataset, together with a species metadata table and a per-genome table of proteome, NLR, and BUSCO statistics, is openly available on Zenodo and Dryad (Toghani et al., 2025b).

Chapter 2/Curation of harmonized plant NLRome datasets on multiple taxonomic resolutions

2.4 Harmonized genome annotation of 346 Solanaceae genomes reveals 197,834 NLR immune receptors

1 figure·4 min read

The third and most finely resolved dataset narrows the scope to a single family. The Solanaceae encompass several agriculturally important crops, including potato, tomato, eggplant, pepper, and tobacco, alongside a rich diversity of wild relatives that serve as reservoirs of genetic variation. I assembled a set of 346 publicly available Solanaceae genomes spanning 85 species and 9 genera. Because many species are represented by multiple independent assemblies, the dataset supports comparison at both the interspecific and the intraspecific level, the resolution on which the analyses developed in later chapters relate to. This release builds directly on an earlier Solanaceae NLRome resource, which cataloged 66,665 NLRs from 124 published Solanaceae proteomes (Sugihara et al., 2023). That earlier dataset relied on heterogeneous, author-supplied annotations and so was subject to the pipeline-to-pipeline inconsistency described above. Here, the sampling was expanded to 346 genomes, and the author-supplied annotations were replaced throughout with harmonized de novo annotations generated using the same Helixer-based workflow applied to the superasterid dataset (Stiehler et al., 2021; Holst et al., 2023; Pertea and Pertea, 2020). NLRs and NLR-associated sequences were identified with NLRtracker (Kourelis et al., 2021) using InterProScan for domain assignment (Blum et al., 2025), and annotation completeness was assessed with BUSCO v6.0.0 against the family-appropriate solanales_odb12 lineage dataset (Manni et al., 2021).

Across the 346 genomes the pipeline predicted 15,078,455 protein sequences, with a median proteome size of 35,970 (interquartile range 32,587–42,519). The harmonized annotations appeared to be of high and consistent quality (Figure 2.4A), with BUSCO completeness averaging 96.6% (median 97.8%), 97.4% of genomes exceeding 90% completeness, and 78.6% exceeding 95%. Both fragmented and missing BUSCOs were low, at a median of 1.0% and 1.1%, respectively. Elevated BUSCO duplication was common, with 49 genomes exceeding 50% duplicated BUSCOs. Because duplicated single-copy orthologs are a recognized signature of polyploidy (Manni et al., 2021), and the Solanaceae include the autotetraploid cultivated potato as well as several other polyploid lineages (Fox et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2025), this pattern most likely reflects the retention of homoeologous gene copies rather than an annotation artifact, though the two cannot be fully disentangled from BUSCO scores alone. Reassuringly, BUSCO completeness showed no correlation with NLR count across the dataset (Pearson r = 0.09), as in the other two collections, which suggests that variation in NLR repertoire size is unlikely to be driven primarily by differences in annotation quality.

Applying the NLRtracker definition, this pipeline recovered 197,834 NLRs. Per-genome counts ranged from 139 to 2,675, with a median of 600 and a mean of 572, and NLRs accounted for a median of 1.44% of each proteome. Within this taxonomically narrow sample, proteome size was more strongly associated with NLR count than in the broader datasets (Pearson r = 0.58; Figure 2.4B), which would be consistent with polyploid genomes tending to carry both more genes overall and more NLRs. At the genus level, the pepper genus Capsicum (n = 30) had the highest median repertoire (630 NLRs), closely followed by Solanum (n = 294; median 610), while Nicotiana (n = 11) carried markedly fewer (median 281) (Figure 2.4C).

The value of this dataset lies in its dense within-species sampling. Nineteen species are represented by more than one genome, including 110 assemblies of Solanum tuberosum (potato), 59 of S. lycopersicum (tomato), and 24 each of Capsicum annuum (pepper) and S. candolleanum. This sampling offers a first view of the extent of intraspecific variation in NLR content (Figure 2.4D). In cultivated tomato, NLR counts were relatively stable across all 59 assemblies (215–244, representing a spread of roughly 13%), which may point to limited presence/absence variation at the species level and to good reproducibility of the harmonized pipeline, although some of this stability could also reflect the comparatively uniform, high-quality assemblies available for tomato. In potato, by contrast, counts ranged far more widely, from 549 to 2,675 across 110 assemblies. This dispersion appears to track the varying ploidy and haplotype content of the potato assemblies, with the highest counts tending to come from genomes with elevated BUSCO duplication, and is therefore probably better interpreted in that light than as straightforward differences in gene copy number. These patterns are suggestive rather than definitive and disentangling true intraspecific variation from assembly- and ploidy-related effects will require the more controlled comparisons developed in the following chapters.

Classifying NLRs by their N-terminal signaling domain gave a breakdown consistent with the other datasets, with CC-NLRs the dominant class (111,968; 56.6%), followed by TIR-NLRs (27,724; 14.0%) and CCR-NLRs / RPW8-type helper NLRs (1,117; 0.6%). A further 16.3% could not be unambiguously resolved among the CC/CCR/CCG10 types, and 12.3% remained undetermined.

The dataset provides the underlying genome assemblies, the complete Helixer-derived annotation outputs (proteome, CDS, and GFF files), and the full NLRtracker output archives, following the same file organization as the superasterid resource. It is openly available on Zenodo (Toghani et al., 2026c) and is intended to serve as a harmonized foundation for comparative genomics, NLR evolution, and immune-receptor engineering in the nightshade family.

Previous2.3 Deep-learning-based annotation of 230 superasterid genomes reveals a harmonized dataset of 91,366 NLRsNext 2.5 Conclusions and Discussion

Chapter 2/Curation of harmonized plant NLRome datasets on multiple taxonomic resolutions

2.5 Conclusions and Discussion

1 min read

In this chapter I curated three NLR datasets spanning nested taxonomic resolutions, together comprising 756 plant genomes and more than 400,000 cataloged NLRs. The three collections were designed to complement one another: 180 RefSeq reference proteomes provide a broad, uniformly annotated view of NLR diversity across the green plant lineage; 230 superasterid genomes narrow the focus to the phylogenetic distribution of the NRC network while increasing sampling density; and 346 Solanaceae genomes add the depth needed to compare NLR repertoires within, as well as between, species. Except for the RefSeq set, which was already annotated to a consistent standard, all genomes were re-annotated de novo with a single Helixer model and processed through an identical NLRtracker pipeline, so that differences between genomes reflect biology rather than the pipeline-to-pipeline heterogeneity that motivated this work.

Across all three datasets, the harmonized annotations were of high completeness, and NLR content was uncorrelated with annotation quality, suggesting that the repertoire variation described here is largely biological in origin. It is important, however, to be clear about what harmonization does and does not achieve. Re-annotating every genome with a single Helixer model makes gene models comparable across the collection, but it does not make them perfect. Like any annotation pipeline, Helixer has its own systematic limitations, and it can over-predict genes in repeat-rich or fragmented assemblies, miss atypical or highly divergent NLRs, and inflate counts in polyploid genomes (Sugihara et al., 2026). The datasets presented here therefore trade per-genome optimality for cross-genome consistency; their value lies in comparability rather than in any claim to be the definitive annotation of a single genome. With these limitations in mind, the collections nonetheless recovered well-established patterns, including the absence of NLRs in green algae and the loss of the TIR-NLR class in monocots, providing confidence that they capture genuine evolutionary signal. Together, they establish a consistent foundation for the comparative and evolutionary analyses performed in the following chapters.

Chapter 3

Functional and molecular evolution of the NLR proteins beyond R-AVR co-evolution

7 sections·10 figures·23 min read

Overview

In this chapter I examined two features of the NRC helper clade that are not easily explained by co-evolution with pathogen effectors: the diversification of the N-terminal MADA motif, and the divergence of the interfaces through which these receptors self-associate in their resting state. In both cases, the relevant selective pressures appear to arise from within the network itself, driven by the requirement that a receptor signals independently and correctly, rather than from direct recognition of pathogen molecules.

About this chapter

Part of the work described in this chapter has been published in Selvaraj et al. (Selvaraj et al., 2024) and appears here with permission. Cryo-EM structure determination was carried out by Muniyandi Selvaraj. Biochemical and cell death assays for NbNRC2 homodimer section were performed by Mauricio Contreras and Muniyandi Selvaraj. My contribution comprised the phylogenomics and the structural analyses described below.

Chapter 3/Functional and molecular evolution of the NLR proteins beyond R-AVR co-evolution

3.1 Introduction

6 min read

Nucleotide-binding and leucine-rich repeat (NLR) immune receptors are essential components of innate immunity across the tree of life, detecting intracellular pathogen components and initiating immune responses to counteract infection (Jones et al., 2016; Contreras et al., 2023a). Plant NLRs are activated by pathogen-secreted virulence proteins, termed effectors, which pathogens deliver into host cells to modulate host physiology (Jones and Dangl, 2006). They belong to the signal transduction ATPases with numerous domains (STAND) superfamily (Leipe et al., 2004) and typically exhibit a tripartite domain architecture consisting of an N-terminal signaling domain, a central nucleotide-binding domain, and C-terminal superstructure-forming repeats (Takken et al., 2006). The central domain, termed NB-ARC (nucleotide-binding adaptor shared by APAF-1, plant R proteins, and CED-4) in plant NLRs, is a signature of this protein family and acts as a molecular switch, mediating the conformational changes required for activation (Takken et al., 2006). A hallmark of NLR activation in eukaryotes and prokaryotes is oligomerization into higher-order immune complexes, termed resistosomes in plants or inflammasomes in mammalian and bacterial cells. These higher order immune complexes initiate immune signaling through diverse mechanisms and often culminate in programmed cell death (Wang et al., 2019b; Bi et al., 2021; Förderer et al., 2022).

Plant NLRs fall into different phylogenetic classes carrying distinct N-terminal domains, of which the coiled-coil (CC) type is the most widespread (Shao et al., 2019). A canonical plant CC-NLR is Arabidopsis thaliana AtZAR1, which is held in a resting monomeric state in complex with its partner pseudokinase RKS1. Perception of its cognate effector AvrAC primes individual AtZAR1 monomers, which leads to ADP to ATP exchange and undergo conformational changes and subsequently assemble into pentameric resistosomes (Wang et al., 2019b; Bi et al., 2021). Following resistosome assembly, CC-NLR oligomers insert into the plasma membrane and act as calcium-permeable channels, initiating immune signaling and cell death, as shown for AtZAR1 and the wheat CC-NLR TmSr35 (Bi et al., 2021; Förderer et al., 2022). NLRs can operate in different configurations: as functional singletons, as sensor–helper pairs, or within more elaborate immune receptor networks (Adachi et al., 2019b; Wu et al., 2017). Functional singletons such as AtZAR1 and TmSr35 combine both effector perception and immune signaling in a single genetic unit (Adachi et al., 2019b; Saintenac et al., 2013). Many other NLRs, however, have subfunctionalized over evolutionary time into sensors dedicated to pathogen perception and helpers that execute immune signaling, as exemplified by the rice NLR pairs Pik-1/Pik-2 and RGA5/RGA4 (Césari et al., 2014; Maqbool et al., 2015). In the NRC (NLR required for cell death) network of solanaceous plants, multiple sensor CC-NLRs signal redundantly through an array of downstream paralogous helper CC-NLRs to confer disease resistance to diverse pathogens and pests, including oomycetes, fungi, nematodes, insects, viruses, and bacteria (Wu et al., 2017; Derevnina et al., 2021). Effector perception by NRC-dependent sensors (NRC-S) triggers conformational changes in their central nucleotide-binding domain that signal to downstream helper NRCs, activating them, and driving their oligomerization into a helper resistosome (Contreras et al., 2022; Contreras et al., 2023c; Ahn et al., 2023; Toghani et al., 2026a). Assembly into a resistosome is a shared endpoint between AtZAR1 and the NRCs, although the NRC assemblies described to date are hexameric or undecameric rather than pentameric (Liu et al., 2023a; Madhuprakash et al., 2024; Seager et al., 2026; Toghani et al., 2026b).

The N-terminal region is central to this activation mechanism. The MADA motif, located in the N-terminal α1 helix of about 20% of all angiosperm CC-NLRs, is required for plasma membrane integration of resistosome and the induction of cell death (Adachi et al., 2019a). This motif, along with related sequences such as the MAEPL motif found in non-flowering plants, is functionally conserved across evolutionarily distant NLRs capable of triggering cell death (Adachi et al., 2019a; Adachi et al., 2023b). MADA-type NLRs include the ancient singleton ZAR1 as well as helper NLRs from distinct phylogenetic clades such as Pik-2 and NRC4, pointing to a shared origin for these CC-NLRs and indicating that the MADA-type α1 helix has been a feature of the family since the emergence of land plants (Adachi et al., 2019a). As sensor NLRs specialized in pathogen detection, however, they appear to have lost or degenerated their MADA motif, rendering them unable to initiate immune signaling on their own. Consistent with this, NRC helpers carry a MADA motif whereas NRC-S do not, and the N-termini of MADA- or MAEPL-containing NLRs can functionally replace the N-terminus of the helper NRC4, while the N-termini of sensor CC-NLRs cannot (Adachi et al., 2019a; Adachi et al., 2023b). These observations fit an evolutionary “use-it-or-lose-it” model, in which the conserved N-terminal motifs of sensor NLRs degenerated once these receptors came to rely on helpers for cell death execution.

NLRs are among the most evolutionarily dynamic families of plant proteins and are under constant pressure to evolve, whether to gain recognition of new pathogen effectors or effector targets, or to evade effector-mediated suppression (Seong et al., 2020; Prigozhin and Krasileva, 2021). This pressure is most often framed in terms of R–AVR co-evolution, which is usually observed in NLR domains involved in effector recognition. Yet the transition from multifunctional singleton ancestors to networks of specialized partners suggests that additional selective pressures act on NLRs (Adachi et al., 2019b; Wu et al., 2017). The division of labor between NRC-S and NRC-H relaxes evolutionary constraints on individual receptors, allowing faster diversification and functional refinement. It helps unlock greater evolutionary flexibility. Sensor NLRs can readily acquire additional domains, such as integrated domains (IDs) or the Solanaceous Domain (SD), to expand their detection capabilities (Jubic et al., 2019; Kourelis et al., 2023). A further layer of complexity comes from NLRs that modulate the activity of other NLRs in ways that do not fit the standard sensor–helper pairing. NRCX, a full-length CC-NLR closely related to the helpers NRC2 and NRC3, is one such case: its N-terminal MADA sequence is non-functional, and silencing it in N. benthamiana leads to autoimmunity that depends on NRC2 and NRC3, but not NRC4 (Adachi et al., 2023a). NRCX therefore appears to have evolved to regulate the activity of its closest paralogs, likely preventing inappropriate activation of their pathways (Adachi et al., 2023a). Modulators of this kind imply that complex network configurations evolved in part to maintain network balance and prevent misregulation, and that NLR evolution is also shaped by relationships among NLRs themselves rather than just by their interactions with pathogens.

Two aspects of these intra-network relationships remain poorly resolved. First, although the MADA motif is functionally important and broadly interchangeable, it is not known how diverse this region is within NRC helper clade, nor whether the degeneration seen in NRCX represents an isolated event or a recurrent evolutionary outcome. Second, the extent to which the model of NLR activation derived from singletons such as AtZAR1 and TmSr35 applies to helper CC-NLRs is unknown. Paralogous helpers within the NRC network signal redundantly yet remain functionally insulated from one another, and how this insulation is achieved at the level of protein–protein interactions has not been addressed.

In this chapter, I examined both questions using the NRC helper clade of the Solanaceae family as a model system. The NRC helpers are massively expanded in this family, form a well-supported clade, and have been established experimentally, making them well suited to comparative analysis. I first analyzed the diversity of the N-terminal MADA motif across the clade. I then turned to the resting state of NRC2, which we recently showed to accumulate in planta as a homodimer rather than a monomer (Selvaraj et al., 2024). I used phylogenomics across the NRC clade to ask whether the interfaces mediating this self-association have diverged between paralogous helpers. Together, these analyses address how NRC helpers and more broadly NLR proteins have evolved not only in response to pathogens, but also in relation to one another and to their compatibility or incompatibility within a shared network.

Chapter 3/Functional and molecular evolution of the NLR proteins beyond R-AVR co-evolution

3.2 The N-terminal MADA motif has diversified in NRC helpers

5 figures·5 min read

3.2.1NRCX carries a signature threonine at the fourth position of its MADA motif3.2.2A subset of NRC4 sequences share the NRCX N-terminal signature3.2.3NRC4t proteins induce cell death as autoactive mutants

While the function and interchangeability of the MADA motif are well established (Adachi et al., 2019a), the sequence variation observed among MADA-containing NLRs, including non-cell-death-inducing variants, points to potential functional divergence within the family (Adachi et al., 2019a; Adachi et al., 2023a). I hypothesized that diversification within the MADA motif could lead to NLR neofunctionalization. To test this, I analyzed the MADA motif diversity across the NRC helper clade, which provides an ideal model system. Using NLRtracker, I constructed an NLRome dataset from 123 Solanaceae proteomes across the genera Nicotiana, Physalis, Capsicum, and Solanum (Kourelis et al., 2021; Sugihara et al., 2023). From phylogenetic analysis, I extracted 1,796 NRC sequences for downstream investigation. NRC helpers are massively expanded in the Solanaceae and form a well-supported clade within CC-type NLRs (Selvaraj et al., 2024; Lee et al., 2021; Goh et al., 2024) (Figure 3.1). Using reference NRC sequences (Kourelis et al., 2021; Adachi et al., 2023a; Oh et al., 2023), I resolved 15 major subclades within the helper clade. Although all NRC helpers possess a recognizable MADA motif, some, such as NRCX (Adachi et al., 2023a), do not induce cell death and instead act as negative modulators (Wu et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2021).

Because the MADA motif resides within the N-terminal α1 helix of CC-NLRs, I implemented a computational pipeline to predict secondary structure using NetSurfP-3.0 (Høie et al., 2022) and extract the α1 helix from each sequence. I then clustered these sequences using MCL (Van Dongen, 2008) and mapped the resulting clusters onto the NRC phylogenetic tree (Figure 3.2). Sequence logos from each cluster were used to compare clades. This unbiased clustering matched the phylogenetic relationships of the NRC helpers and revealed that the N-terminal α1 helix has diversified in both length and amino acid composition.

3.2.1 NRCX carries a signature threonine at the fourth position of its MADA motif

Building on previous observations that chimeras between the NRCX N-terminus and NRC4 fail to induce cell death (Adachi et al., 2023a), I compared N-terminal sequences of the NRCX clade with its sister clades, NRC2 and NRC3. NRCX carries a conserved threonine at the fourth position of its MADA motif (T4) that is absent in both NRC2 and NRC3 (Figure 3.3A). I hypothesized that this T4 residue represents a degenerative mutation that renders the MADA motif of NRCX incapable of triggering cell death.

3.2.2 A subset of NRC4 sequences share the NRCX N-terminal signature

Prompted by the identification of the NRCX T4 signature, I screened other NRC clades for the same feature. The T4 signature was also present in the NRC4/5 superclade (Figure 3.3B). Mapping these sequences onto the NRC phylogeny revealed that most NRC4 variants carrying the T4 residue belong to a distinct subclade sister to NRC4a (Figure 3.4). I designated this subclade as “NRC4t”. The NRC4t clade mirrors NRCX in two aspects: it forms a distinct lineage closely related to a canonical helper clade (NRC4a), and it carries the characteristic T4 N-terminal signature.

3.2.3 NRC4t proteins induce cell death as autoactive mutants

Given their N-terminal sequence similarity to NRCX, I tested whether representative NRC4t proteins are competent to trigger cell death. I hypothesized that, like NRCX, NRC4t variants would fail to induce cell death as autoactive mutants due to the T4 substitution. To test this, I transiently expressed two potato NRC4t variants (StNRC4p and StNRC4h) alongside autoactive mutants carrying a D-to-V substitution in the MHD motif, and screened for cell death (constructs cloned and provided by Jiorgos Kourelis; Table 3.1).

Contrary to the initial hypothesis, both NRC4t DV mutants also induced strong cell death, while their wild-type variants did not cause any visible cell death. To confirm this finding and exclude interference from endogenous helpers, I repeated the assay across two independent replicates in an nrc2/3/4 knockout line of N. benthamiana, and obtained consistent results (Figure 3.5B). NbNRC4, a potato NRC4a homolog (StNRC4e), NbNRCX, and StNRCX, together with their corresponding DV mutants, served as controls: wild-type proteins were not expected to cause cell death, NRCX DV mutants served as negative controls (Adachi et al., 2023a), and NRC4 DV mutants served as positive controls. The controls behaved as expected: StNRCX did not cause cell death, whereas StNRC4e triggered cell death as an autoactive DV mutant (Figure 3.5A). These findings demonstrate that NRC4t receptors do not behave like NRCX in this assay; whether they operate as canonical helpers or fulfill specialized regulatory roles on other NRC helpers remains to be determined.

3.3 Resting-state NRC2 forms a homodimer

1 figure·2 min read

Recently, we showed that NbNRC2, unlike the canonical functional singleton NbZAR1, self-associates in co-immunoprecipitation assays (Figure 3.6A) (Selvaraj et al., 2024). Moreover, we could not detect hetero-association between NbNRC2 and its paralogs NbNRC3 and NbNRC4, or NbZAR1. This suggests that NbNRC2 preferentially self-associates in N. benthamiana and does not form stable heterocomplexes with its paralogs. This conclusion was independently corroborated by live-cell confocal microscopy showing that resting-state NbNRC2 and NbNRC4 do not co-localize in planta (Selvaraj et al., 2024).

To investigate the NbNRC2 resting state we performed cryo-EM 2D class averaging (Figure 3.6B) and resolved the atomic model of the resting-state NbNRC2 homodimer. The cryo-EM model included the NBD, HD1-WHD, and LRR domains, while the N-terminal CC domain was absent from the density (Figure 3.6C) (Selvaraj et al., 2024). This structure revealed the contact sites between the two protomers, comprising eight stretches that form three main interaction interfaces across the NBD, HD1-WHD, and LRR domains (Figure 3.6C,D) (Selvaraj et al., 2024). Because NbNRC2 does not form stable heterocomplexes with other NRC paralogs despite their shared evolutionary origin, we hypothesized that these homodimerization interfaces diversified across NRC helpers to insulate their association and therefore activation pathways.

3.4 Evolution of homodimerization in NRCs

1 figure·3 min read

3.4.1The dimerization interfaces have diverged between NRC clades3.4.2Entropy analysis reveals clade-specific variation in NRC homodimerization stretches

To test whether the homodimerization interfaces have diversified across NRC helpers, I performed a phylogenomic analysis across the expanded NRC clade of the Solanaceae. Using the 123-proteome Solanaceae NLRome dataset (Sugihara et al., 2023), phylogenetic analysis yielded 993 unique NRC sequences. Together with 99 reference NRC sequences from N. benthamiana, C. annuum, S. lycopersicum, and S. tuberosum, these were used to construct a detailed phylogenetic tree of the NRC helper clade. This resolved the 15 subclades noted above, with clade sizes ranging from 31 to 129 sequences.

3.4.1 The dimerization interfaces have diverged between NRC clades

When I compared the eight dimerization stretches identified in the NbNRC2 homodimer (Selvaraj et al., 2024) across all NRC sequences, they were noticeably less conserved than classic NLR motifs such as the P-loop and MHD (Figure 3.7A). This suggests that these interfaces diversified during NRC evolution. Within individual NRC clades, however, these regions were substantially more conserved (Figure 3.7B).

To quantify this, I calculated the relative amino acid ratio within each major clade (NRC2, NRC3, NRC4) compared with the others, using a 50-fold cutoff and requiring at least 80% of sequences within a clade to carry the identified variant (scripts provided by Yu Sugihara). With this analysis I identified clade-unique polymorphisms. For example, the NRC2 and NRC3 clades, which contain the representative proteins tested in the co-immunoprecipitation assays, showed 5 and 3 unique polymorphisms, respectively, across the 44 amino acids comprising the homodimer interface (Figure 3.7B).

3.4.2 Entropy analysis reveals clade-specific variation in NRC homodimerization stretches

To evaluate these patterns further, I used Shannon entropy analysis to quantify position-specific amino acid diversity. In this metric, a fully conserved position has an entropy score of 0, whereas a position with all 20 amino acids occurring at equal probability reaches a maximum entropy of 4.32 bits. I set a threshold of 1.5 bits to identify highly variable positions, following previous studies (Prigozhin and Krasileva, 2021).

All eight dimerization stretches scored above 1.5 bits when all 1,092 NRC sequences were analyzed together, but remained conserved within 11 of the 15 individual NRC clades (Figure 3.S1 and Figure 3.S2). In six clades (NRC0, NRCX, NRC2, NRC3, NRC4a, and NRC4t), all residues across the eight stretches scored below the 1.5-bit threshold, showing little to no sequence diversity. In five clades (NRC1, NRC6, NRC7, NRC4b, and NRC4other), the eight stretches remained below this threshold except for one to three variable residues per clade. In the remaining four clades (NRC8, NRC9, NRC5, and NRC4c), the stretches contained up to 12 variable residues with entropy values above 1.5 bits, reflecting higher sequence divergence. In contrast, the catalytic P-loop and MHD motifs remained below the 1.5-bit cutoff in 13 of the 15 clades, displaying minimal sequence variation (Figure 3.S1 and Figure 3.S2).

Chapter 3/Functional and molecular evolution of the NLR proteins beyond R-AVR co-evolution

3.5 Conclusions and Discussion

1 figure·5 min read

In this chapter I examined two features of the NRC helper clade that are not easily explained by co-evolution with pathogen effectors: the diversification of the N-terminal MADA motif, and the divergence of the interfaces through which these receptors self-associate in their resting state. In both cases, the relevant selective pressures appear to arise from within the network itself, driven by the requirement that a receptor signals independently and correctly, rather than from direct recognition of pathogen molecules.

The MADA analysis began from the observation that while all NRC helpers carry the motif, not all of them execute cell death. Unbiased clustering of N-terminal α1 helix sequences recovered the phylogenetic structure of the clade and showed that the α1 helix has diversified in both length and sequence. This is notable for a region whose function is generally considered interchangeable between distantly related NLRs (Adachi et al., 2019a). Within this diversity, NRCX carries a threonine at the fourth position (T4) of the motif that is absent from its closest functional relatives, NRC2 and NRC3. Our working hypothesis was that this T4 residue represents a degenerative substitution that renders the MADA motif non-functional, consistent with the inability of NRCX to trigger cell death and with the loss of activity in NRCX–NRC4 N-terminal chimeras (Adachi et al., 2023a).

Screening for this signature across the wider clade revealed that it is not unique to NRCX. Around a quarter of NRC4/5 sequences also carry the T4 signature, and most of these form a distinct subclade, NRC4t, that is sister to NRC4a in much the same way that NRCX sits sister to NRC2 and NRC3. Given this parallel in both sequence and phylogenetic placement, I hypothesized that NRC4t might represent a second, independently derived group of modulators.

However, functional assays did not support this idea. Both potato NRC4t variants tested induced strong cell death as autoactive mutants, both in wild-type plants and in nrc2/3/4 knockout line, behaving like canonical helper NLRs like NRC2 and NRC4. Moreover, I could detect the T4 pattern in other NRC4 and NRC5 proteins not belonging to NRC4t clade. Additionally, not all NRC4t clade sequences contained the T4 signature. The most direct interpretation is that the T4 substitution alone is not sufficient to abolish cell death activity, and that the functional degeneration of NRCX depends on additional features within its N-terminus or elsewhere in the protein. This is supported by lack of cell death with NRCX chimeras containing NRC4 α1 (Adachi et al., 2023a). Whether NRC4t proteins act as conventional helpers or have acquired distinct regulatory roles remains an open question. This will require identifying the upstream NRC-S that signal through them or helpers being regulated by them.

In the second half of the chapter, I addressed the homodimer resting state of NRC2. NRC2 accumulates in planta as a homodimer and does not form stable heterocomplexes with the paralogs NRC3 and NRC4, despite their shared evolutionary origin and overlapping roles in the network (Selvaraj et al., 2024). The phylogenomic data support that expectation. Across all 1,092 NRC sequences, the eight dimerization stretches were markedly less conserved than the P-loop and MHD motifs, suggesting that they diversified as the clade expanded. Within individual clades, however, these stretches were well conserved. Each of the major clades also carried unique polymorphisms at these positions. This pattern of between-clade divergence combined with within-clade conservation matches what is expected when selection acts to preserve self-association while preventing cross-association between paralogs, paralleling theoretical models for the emergence of orthogonal signaling pathways following gene duplication (Capra et al., 2012; McClune and Laub, 2020).

Together with the structural data, these findings suggest that the diversification of dimerization interfaces serves to insulate helper nodes from one another within the network. Such insulation maintains functional redundancy, minimizes undesired cross-activation between pathways, and provides a way to evade pathogen effectors that suppress individual helpers (Derevnina et al., 2021; Contreras et al., 2023b).

However, several caveats apply to these conclusions. The phylogenomic analyses draw exclusively on Solanaceae genomes, and the 15 clades differ substantially in size, meaning the entropy and polymorphism comparisons are not equally powered across all clades. Furthermore, co-immunoprecipitation captures stable complexes and would not necessarily detect weak or transient interactions between paralogs, which may still occur during activation and release. Most importantly, the link between interface divergence and activation insulation remains correlative. The sequence analyses show that these positions have diverged in the expected pattern, but do not directly prove that this divergence prevents heterodimerization. Although stretch swaps between NbNRC2a and NbNRC3 lead to loss of association between the NRC2 chimera and the WT variant (Selvaraj et al., 2024), testing will require swapping or mutating interface residues between paralogs to determine whether heterodimerization is acquired.

A further consideration links the two themes of this chapter. Tomato NRC2 has recently been shown to assemble beyond the homodimer, forming tetramers and higher-order oligomers at elevated concentrations in an inactive conformation. Dimerization and higher-order oligomerization appear to stabilize the resting state, sequestering the receptor from assembling into an active resistosome, while mutations at the dimeric or interdimeric interfaces enhance pathogen-induced cell death (Ma et al., 2024). However, we could not detect a tetramer for NbNRC2 resting state.

In the SlNRC2 tetramer, two homodimers associate through an interface distinct from the dimerization contacts analyzed above. This contact is formed by residues at the N-terminus of the CC domain of one protomer (including M14, R18, and D32) packing against the LRR domain of an adjacent protomer at positions including Y739 and T743 (Figure 3.8). Notably, the CC residues involved fall directly within or adjacent to the N-terminal α1 helix carrying the MADA motif. If this arrangement is functional in vivo, this region would serve two distinct roles: executing cell death upon activation and maintaining the resting receptor in an autoinhibited higher-order state prior to activation. Whether this tetramerization interface is general to the NRC clade or specific to NRC2 remains unresolved. Moreover, why NRCs dimerize or why NLRs can exist as monomers, dimers, and higher oligomers in their resting state remains unanswered here.

More broadly, these results illustrate that NLR evolution is shaped by internal network dynamics as well as by arms races with pathogens. The interfaces examined here reside within the N-terminal, NB-ARC, and LRR regions that mediate self-association and oligomerization, rather than the interfaces that bind effectors. The pressures acting on them stem from the need to maintain functional architecture within the network.

Chapter 4

Contrasting patterns of evolution in sensor and helper NLRs

7 sections·17 figures·24 min read

Overview

In this chapter, I address three primary questions: how extensively the NRC network has expanded in the Asterales relative to the Solanales, and how its members are arranged in the genome; whether a functional sensor–helper network operates in lettuce; and whether helpers and distinct sensor subgroups exhibit different signatures of selection within the genus Lactuca. Building on the harmonized annotation framework developed in Chapter 2, I show that the network is comparatively less expanded in the Asterales. Nevertheless, lettuce maintains a functional, partially redundant network supported by two helpers. Furthermore, NRC-S dependent on the ancient helper NRC0, which reflects the ancestral state of the NRC network, evolve under markedly stronger constraint than those that have shifted onto more derived helpers.

About this chapter

The work described in this chapter has been published in Pai et al. (Pai et al., 2026) and appears here with permission. Cell death assays were performed by Hsuan Pai. I carried out the bioinformatic and evolutionary analyses and generated all the figures.

Chapter 4/Contrasting patterns of evolution in sensor and helper NLRs

4.1 Introduction

5 min read

Plants rely on a layered innate immune system to defend themselves against a broad range of pathogens (Jones and Dangl, 2006; Dodds et al., 2024). Intracellular NLR receptors form a central component of this system, recognizing pathogen-secreted effector proteins and initiating defense responses that often culminate in localized programmed cell death to restrict pathogen spread (Jones and Dangl, 2006). NLRs constitute one of the most diverse protein families in plants, with individual members evolving at strikingly different rates (Prigozhin and Krasileva, 2021; Michelmore and Meyers, 1998; Seong et al., 2020). What remains poorly resolved is how much of this variation in evolutionary tempo reflects the specific functional role a given receptor plays.

NLRs typically exhibit a tripartite architecture: an N-terminal signaling domain, most often a coiled-coil (CC) or Toll/interleukin-1 receptor (TIR) domain; a central NB-ARC domain that governs activation; and a C-terminal leucine-rich repeat (LRR) domain that mediates pathogen detection either directly or indirectly (Kourelis et al., 2021). Based on NB-ARC phylogeny, they fall into four main classes: CC-NLRs, CCG10-NLRs, RPW8-type CCR-NLRs, and TIR-NLRs (Kourelis et al., 2021). This architecture is not invariant; a subset of receptors carry additional integrated domains that act as decoys or baits for effector recognition (Kroj et al., 2016; Sarris et al., 2016). Approximately 20% of CC-NLRs also carry a conserved N-terminal MADA motif required for cell death execution (Adachi et al., 2019a). Upon activation, CC-NLRs assemble into higher-order complexes termed resistosomes, which insert into the plasma membrane to act as calcium-permeable channels via their N-terminal helices (Wang et al., 2019a; Bi et al., 2021). Recent computational advances now allow such assemblies to be modeled in simulated membrane environments with high confidence (Selvaraj et al., 2024; Toghani et al., 2025a).

Many NLRs do not act autonomously. Some function as genetically linked pairs, such as the rice CC-NLR pairs Pik-1/Pik-2 and RGA5/RGA4, or the Arabidopsis thaliana TIR-NLR pair RPS4/RRS1 (Kroj et al., 2016; Sarris et al., 2016). Others are organized into wider networks where sensors depend on helpers in one-to-many or many-to-one configurations (Adachi et al., 2019b). The CCR-NLRs NRG1 and ADR1 act downstream of TIR-NLR signaling in this manner (Castel et al., 2019; Saile et al., 2020).

The NRC network, first described in solanaceous species such as tomato and Nicotiana benthamiana, is the best-characterized CC-NLR network. Sensor NLRs (NRC-S) detect effectors but cannot signal independently, depending instead on helper NLRs (NRC-H) to transduce signals and execute cell death (Wu et al., 2017; Adachi et al., 2019b). NRC-S fall into two structural subtypes: Rx-type NRC-S with canonical domain architecture, and SD-type NRC-S carrying an additional N-terminal Solanaceous domain (Seong et al., 2020). Upon effector detection, sensors trigger the transition of their helpers from a resting homodimer into hexameric resistosomes (Contreras et al., 2022; Ahn et al., 2023; Selvaraj et al., 2024). The mechanism transmitting this signal between sensor and helper is consistent with a transient activation-and-release interaction rather than a stable, persistent complex (Contreras et al., 2022; Ahn et al., 2023; Contreras et al., 2024).

The network is thought to have emerged roughly 100 million years ago in the superasterid lineage and has expanded to varying degrees across asterid families, reaching its greatest complexity in the lamiids (Wu et al., 2017; Goh et al., 2024; Sakai et al., 2024). Within the network, NRC0 stands out as the most ancient and conserved helper and is frequently linked genetically to the NRC-S that depend on it. In contrast, derived helpers have undergone lineage-specific expansions and occupy varied genomic positions, with some clustered alongside NRC-S, such as NRC6, and others dispersed (Goh et al., 2024; Sakai et al., 2024; Lee et al., 2021).

The broad generalization in the field is that NRC-S evolve rapidly while helpers remain conserved (Goh et al., 2024). However, as shown in Chapter 3, paralogous helpers are themselves subject to diversifying selection that preserves homodimerization while preventing cross-activation between paralogs (Selvaraj et al., 2024). This variation in evolutionary tempo is not arbitrary. NLR repertoires range from a handful to over a thousand genes per genome and follow a birth-and-death model, where duplication continually generates new receptors, some of which are retained for recognition while others are lost or pseudogenized (Michelmore and Meyers, 1998; Seong et al., 2020). On the other hand, pathogens have evolved to target plant immune receptors. The Solanaceae helper NLRs NRC2 and NRC3 are suppressed by the cyst nematode effector SS15 and the oomycete effector AVRcap1b (Derevnina et al., 2021). In return, in some species NRC3 has accumulated mutations in the effector-binding loop that allows evading suppression (Sugihara et al., 2025). Redundancy within the network ensures that unsuppressed nodes maintain signaling when others are blocked (Derevnina et al., 2021). Under this model helpers face multiple evolutionary constraints. They need to retain compatibility with multiple upstream NRC-S while evading pathogen effectors that target them.

Most of our knowledge about the network derives from the Solanaceae family, leaving open the question of whether its architecture and evolutionary dynamics are general asterid features or specific to that family. The Asterales, a campanulid order that includes lettuce (Lactuca sativa), offer a useful comparison. Lettuce is a classic model for resistance genetics. Its NLR repertoire was organized by Meyers and colleagues into 42 phylogenetic Resistance Gene Candidate (RGC) groups, later consolidated into eight Major Resistance Clusters (MRCs) distributed across six chromosomes (Meyers et al., 1998; McHale et al., 2009; Christopoulou et al., 2015). Early work on the lettuce RGC2 locus distinguished two NLR classes: a diverse type I and a conserved type II, with contrasting copy numbers and evolutionary trajectories (Kuang et al., 2004). This distinction has since been recognized in other systems, including Arabidopsis thaliana and maize (Prigozhin and Krasileva, 2021). Despite this rich background in resistance genetics, the NRC network in the Asterales has received little attention.

In this chapter, I address three primary questions: how extensively the NRC network has expanded in the Asterales relative to the Solanales, and how its members are arranged in the genome; whether a functional sensor–helper network operates in lettuce; and whether helpers and distinct sensor subgroups exhibit different signatures of selection within the genus Lactuca. Building on the harmonized annotation framework developed in Chapter 2, I show that the network is comparatively less expanded in the Asterales. Nevertheless, lettuce maintains a functional, partially redundant network supported by two helpers. Furthermore, NRC-S dependent on the ancient helper NRC0, which reflects the ancestral state of the NRC network, evolve under markedly stronger constraint than those that have shifted onto more derived helpers.

Chapter 4/Contrasting patterns of evolution in sensor and helper NLRs

4.2 The NRC network has expanded less in Asterales relative to Solanales

1 figure·2 min read

Because the NRC network is distributed across the asterids, I first compared its gene content between the Solanales (a lamiid order) and the Asterales (a campanulid order) (Figure 4.1A) (Wu et al., 2017). Applying NLRtracker (Kourelis et al., 2021) to 40 Solanales and 29 Asterales genomes that I annotated with Helixer (Stiehler et al., 2021; Holst et al., 2023), yielded 21,232 non-redundant NLR sequences. Phylogenetic analysis of these sequences alongside RefPlantNLR references led to identification of the NRC network as a group of 7,020 sequences (Figure 4.S1) (Kourelis et al., 2021).

Total NLR content was broadly comparable between the two orders, averaging 300 sequences per genome in the Asterales and 338.6 in the Solanales. The proportion accounted for by the NRC network, however, differed: NRC-type receptors represented on average only 6.6% of the Asterales NLRome, compared with 50.3% in the Solanales (Figure 4.S2). While both orders carry comparable numbers of NLRs overall, the Asterales have expanded other NLR classes instead of the NRC network.

To resolve this pattern, I analyzed the 592 Asterales NRC network sequences, which comprise 88 helpers and 504 NRC-S (Figure 4.1B). The helpers split into two phylogroups: 27 sequences grouped with NRC0, while the remaining 61 formed a distinct clade alongside known Solanales helpers (such as NRC2 and NRC4), hereafter referred to as Ast-NRCs (Wu et al., 2017). All 504 Asterales NRC-S clustered in a single well-supported clade sister to Solanales SD-type NRC-S. None grouped with the Rx-type NRC-S prominent in the Solanales. Although these Asterales NRC-S are phylogenetically SD-type, they lack the N-terminal Solanaceous domain itself.

I observed the same patterns in lettuce. Its 17 NRC sequences (two helpers and 15 NRC-S) represent only 5% of its NLRome consisting of 359 NLRs. Instead, the repertoire is dominated by TIR-NLRs (206 sequences, over 57%). The CC-NLR, CCR-NLR, and CCG10-NLR classes each have 97, 9, and 42 sequences, respectively (Figure 4.S3). NLR expansion in lettuce has therefore been highly uneven, with the NRC network remaining among the least expanded.

4.3 Asterales NRC networks show lineage-specific expansion and variable genomic clustering

1 figure·2 min read

Given the differences between the two orders, I next examined the copy number and genomic organization of the network within the Asterales in more detail, focusing on Lactuca. I analyzed 40 helper and sensor sequences drawn from common lettuce and two wild relatives, Lactuca saligna and Lactuca virosa. Phylogenetic analysis resolved these into four well-supported groups: a single helper group containing sequences phylogenetically clustering either to NRC0 or to tomato NRC2 (termed Ast-NRC1 in each species), and three sensor groups, hereafter referred to as groups 1, 2, and 3 (Figure 4.2A). Mapping these onto the established lettuce NLR classification showed that they correspond to four previously defined RGC groups: the helpers to RGC7, and sensor groups 1, 2, and 3 to RGC26, RGC27, and RGC9, respectively (Figure 4.S3) (Meyers et al., 1998; McHale et al., 2009).

Because NRC-H and NRC-S often occur in genetic clusters, as reported for NRC0 and for Solanaceae NRC6 (Sakai et al., 2024; Lee et al., 2021), I mapped these genes onto the lettuce chromosomes. Contrary to the pattern observed in other asterids, LsatNRC0 on chromosome 3 is isolated from any sensor sequence (Figure 4.2B) (Sakai et al., 2024). Ast-LsatNRC1, by contrast, resides within a physical cluster of less than 100 kb on chromosome 8 alongside NRC-S from groups 2 and 3, with all group 3 members localized to this locus. This cluster falls within the previously described MRC8c locus (Christopoulou et al., 2015; McHale et al., 2009). The remaining NRC-S, including all of group 1, are dispersed across chromosomes 4, 8, and 9 within MRC4, MRC8a, and MRC9a. LsatNRC0 is the only NRC gene outside any reported MRC.

The lack of chromosome-level assemblies for the wild lettuce species precluded a complete synteny analysis, although Ast-LvirNRC1 was located adjacent to group 2 and 3 NRC-S on a single contig (Figure 4.S4). Given these observations, I extended this analysis to five additional Asterales species, classified by their phylogenetic relationship to Lactuca helpers and NRC-S (Figure 4.S5), revealed no uniform genomic arrangement. In Cichorium intybus, CiNRC0 lies within 500 kb of a group 1 sensor, while both Ast-CiNRC1 copies cluster with group 2 and 3 NRC-S. In Cynara cardunculus, CcNRC0 is close to a group 1 sensor and Ast-CcNRC1 clusters with four group 1 NRC-S. In contrast, in Helianthus annuus, Chrysanthemum lavandulifolium, and Codonopsis lanceolata, helpers and NRC-S show no genomic clustering (Figures 4.S6 and 4.S7). Physical linkage within the network is therefore variable both within Lactuca and across the wider Asterales order.

Chapter 4/Contrasting patterns of evolution in sensor and helper NLRs

4.4 LsatNRC0 and Ast-LsatNRC1 signal for distinct sensor groups

1 figure·2 min read

To test whether the phylogenetic grouping of these sequences into NRC-H and NRC-S reflects genuine functional dependency, we used Agrobacterium-mediated transient co-expression in an nrc2/3/4 CRISPR knockout line of Nicotiana benthamiana (Wu et al., 2017). Because the cognate effectors of these lettuce NRC-S are unknown, we generated autoactive derivatives carrying a D-to-V substitution in the MHD motif (Adachi et al., 2019a). Expressed alone, none of the NRC-S produced a visible cell death response, whereas autoactive variants of both helpers triggered strong cell death in Nicotiana benthamiana leaves (Figure 4.S8).

NRC-S and NRC-H were then co-expressed pairwise. Of the 16 NRC-S tested, nine induced visible cell death when combined with one or both wild-type helpers, and these phenotypes were reproducible across replicates (Figure 4.S8). These functional dependencies mapped cleanly onto the phylogeny: three NRC-S signaled exclusively through LsatNRC0 and all belonged to group 1; four signaled exclusively through Ast-LsatNRC1 and all belonged to group 3; and two NRC-S from group 2 could induce cell death with either helper (Figure 4.3A).

I also screened these sequences for the MADA motif required for helper-mediated cell death (Adachi et al., 2019a). Both helpers encoded clear MADA motifs, whereas none of the NRC-S did, matching the observation that only the helpers can execute cell death independently.

Functional dependencies in the wild lettuce species and across the wider Asterales remain to be validated experimentally. However, given their phylogenetic relationships and the fact that both NRC0 and group 1 NRC-S are absent from several of these genomes, functional specificity likely follows the same group-wise pattern. Together, these results define a functional NRC network in lettuce in which two helpers work downstream of nine NRC-S with partial redundancy (Figure 4.3B).
