Chapter 4/Contrasting patterns of evolution in sensor and helper NLRs

4.5 NRC-S dependent on Ast-LsatNRC1 are under stronger positive selection

1 figure·3 min read

To determine whether these functional differences are reflected in distinct selective regimes, I tested for positive selection across the Lactuca NRC groups using CodeML in PAML suite (Yang, 1997). These analyses compare a model permitting a subset of sites to evolve under positive selection (ω = dN/dS  > 1) against a null model with neutral and purifying selection only (ω ≤ 1). Where the selection model fits significantly better, individual sites under positive selection are identified by Bayes Empirical Bayes (BEB) analysis (Yang, 2005). For each group, I compared model M8 against its null counterpart M8a using a likelihood ratio test.

For the helpers, the test was not significant at the 1% threshold (p = 0.037), and BEB identified no positively selected sites. Sensor group 2 yielded a statistically significant likelihood ratio test (p = 0.003) but likewise lacked any BEB-supported sites. A significant test in the absence of identified sites is most conservatively interpreted as a false positive, as the M8a/M8 comparison is sensitive to alignment noise and gene conversion.

Sensor groups 1 and 3, by contrast, showed clear signatures of positive selection. In group 1, BEB identified five sites with posterior probabilities exceeding 0.95, three of which mapped to the CC domain on an AlphaFold 3 structural model (Figure 4.4B). Group 3 displayed the strongest signal, with 48 sites above 0.95 and 33 exceeding 0.99 posterior probability. The majority of these sites mapped to the concave face of the LRR domain, the surface typically responsible for direct effector recognition (Figure 4.4C) (Prigozhin and Krasileva, 2021).

To test whether average selective pressure varies across groups, I fitted a branch model assigning an independent ω to each phylogroup and compared it to a uniform one-ratio model. The four-ratio model fit the data significantly better (2 ⋅ Δln L = 305.66, df  = 3, p = 6.5 × 10−65), yielding ω = 0.12 for the helpers, 0.35 for group 1, 0.39 for group 2, and 0.58 for group 3. The helpers showed the lowest average ω and group 3 the highest, matching the site-level analyses (Figure 4.S9). Although the four groups differ in sequence count and tree depth, their total tree dS lengths are comparable (1.51–2.87), as the higher sequence number in group 3 is offset by lower per-branch divergence. Branch-level heterogeneity under the free-ratio model is shown for reference in Figure 4.S10.

Finally, I calculated pairwise dN, dS, and ω values within each group using the Nei–Gojobori method, both across full-length sequences and separately for the CC, NB-ARC, and LRR domains (Figure 4.S11) (Nei and Gojobori, 1986). The helper group consistently had the lowest average ω. Sensor group 3 showed the highest overall ratios, while the CC domain of group 1 NRC-S yielded pairwise ω > 1, indicating domain-specific positive selection rates (Figure 4.S12). Together, these analyses indicate that NRC-S signaling through Ast-LsatNRC1 evolve under stronger positive selection than those dependent on LsatNRC0, while the helpers themselves remain under strong purifying constraint.

Previous4.4 LsatNRC0 and Ast-LsatNRC1 signal for distinct sensor groupsNext 4.6 Conclusions and discussion

Chapter 4/Contrasting patterns of evolution in sensor and helper NLRs

4.6 Conclusions and discussion

1 figure·6 min read

Using the harmonized annotations described in Chapter 2, in this chapter I compared the NRC network between two asterid orders and used lettuce as a model to study the evolution of NRC network. Although the Asterales and Solanales carry comparable numbers of NLRs per genome, the NRC network accounts for only 6.6% of the Asterales repertoire compared with 50.3% in the Solanales. The Asterales have expanded other classes instead, most conspicuously the TIR-NLRs, which alone make up more than half of the lettuce NLRome. This fits the wider observation that the network proliferated heavily in lamiids relative to campanulids (Goh et al., 2024).

I observed the absence of Rx-type NRC-S from the Asterales. This group expanded extensively in the Solanales and contains many of the characterized resistance genes in solanaceous crops (Wu et al., 2017). The Asterales NRC-S cluster phylogenetically with Solanales SD-type NRC-S yet lack the Solanaceous domain itself. It has been proposed that this pattern reflects the secondary loss of SD-containing NRC-S in the Asterales (Seong et al., 2020). Consistent with this, the presence of SD-like NRC-S in more distantly related superasterids, such as sugar beet, argues that NRC-S with and without this integration were already present in their common ancestor, with the SD-carrying forms subsequently lost in ancestral Asterales. Resolving this will require denser phylogenetic sampling across the superasterids to determine when and how the SD integration originally arose.

Within lettuce, the network resolves into one helper and three sensor groups that map onto four previously described RGC groups (Meyers et al., 1998). Ast-LsatNRC1, together with all group 3 NRC-S and one group 2 sensor, lies within MRC8c, a cluster associated with quantitative trait loci for resistance to Fusarium oxysporum and Verticillium dahliae (Christopoulou et al., 2015). NRC-type receptors account for 12 of the 26 immune receptor genes at that locus. Although they have not yet been directly implicated in lettuce disease resistance.

The remaining NRC-S fall within MRC4, MRC8a, and MRC9a, of which MRC4 and MRC9a have been linked to downy mildew resistance (Christopoulou et al., 2015; McHale et al., 2009). LsatNRC0 sits outside any reported MRC and, unlike its homologs in several other asterids, is unlinked to any sensor (Sakai et al., 2024). Together with the variable genomic clustering observed across the other Asterales species surveyed here, this suggests that the ancient linkage of NRC0 to its NRC-S was disrupted by lineage-specific genomic rearrangements rather than lost systematically.

The functional assays extend earlier phylogenetic surveys of NRC network architecture (Goh et al., 2024) by directly testing which NRC-S signal through each helper. They reveal a graded shift in helper dependency across the sensor phylogeny: exclusive reliance on ancestral NRC0 in group 1, dual compatibility in group 2, and exclusive dependence on the derived Ast-LsatNRC1 in group 3. This makes lettuce a useful experimental system, as it allows helper dependency and evolutionary rate to be compared within a single, compact network rather than across distantly related species.

The selection analyses show that these functional categories track evolutionary rate: helpers are under the strongest purifying selection, group 1 NRC-S show limited diversification, and group 3 NRC-S display strong signatures of positive selection concentrated on the concave LRR surface implicated in effector binding.

The low sequence variability of the helpers matches observations from other helper systems, such as ADR1, which likewise belongs to the low-variability NLR class (Prigozhin and Krasileva, 2021; Saile et al., 2020). Group 1 NRC-S are unusual in having their variability concentrated within the CC domain and the N-terminal portion of the LRR rather than the typical recognition interfaces, consistent with previous observations on NRC0-dependent NRC-S (Sakai et al., 2024); whether this pattern reflects relaxed selection or an active co-evolutionary process remains an open question. Group 2 NRC-S are comparatively invariant and represent the intermediate group capable of signaling through either helper. In contrast, group 3 NRC-S resemble highly polymorphic receptors such as Arabidopsis thaliana RPP1, displaying multiple positively selected sites clustered on the concave face of the LRR (Prigozhin and Krasileva, 2021).

A plausible model is that evolutionary constraint is shaped by signaling within the network (Figure 4.5). NRC-S that depend on the conserved NRC0 helper may be constrained both by the requirement to maintain helper compatibility and by the nature of their recognition targets, particularly if they monitor conserved effectors or guard essential host targets in a manner similar to the ZAR1–ZRK system. NRC-S that shifted onto a more recently derived helper appear relieved of these constraints, and their physical clustering indicates that recent tandem duplication accelerated their diversification. This pattern is visible in both orders, but is amplified in the Solanales, where a larger suite of derived, lineage-specific helpers supports a greatly expanded set of rapidly diversifying NRC-S. These interpretations should be treated with appropriate caution, as recent duplications and uneven group sizes introduce phylogenetic non-independence and sampling biases that site- and branch-model tests cannot completely eliminate.

The functional data also speak to the biochemical distinction between the two classes. None of the lettuce NRC-S triggered cell death when expressed alone, whereas both helpers did, and multiple lines of biochemical evidence indicate that NRC-dependent NRC-S likewise fail to form higher-order complexes either before or after activation (Contreras et al., 2022; Ahn et al., 2023; Contreras et al., 2024; Selvaraj et al., 2024). Taken together this is consistent with the view that these NRC-S have lost the capacity to assemble resistosomes altogether. Structural modeling supports the same conclusion and is developed in Chapter 6, where the lettuce network is placed alongside monocot NLR pairs to ask whether sensor and helper identity can be predicted structurally.

Why, then, should members of a single network evolve at such different rates? The most economical explanation is that evolutionary trajectory follows from functional position, and specifically from the dependencies each receptor must maintain (Figure 4.5). NRC0 and its dependent NRC-S are conserved across most asterid lineages (Goh et al., 2024; Sakai et al., 2024). Their low copy number and the conservation of their LRR domains, the region that normally mediates recognition, may indicate that they detect conserved effector molecules or guard essential host components in the manner of the ZAR1–ZRK system (Adachi et al., 2023b), either of which would limit how far the receptor can drift. A second, non-exclusive constraint is the requirement to remain compatible with NRC0 itself, since changes that compromise signaling to the helper would be selected against. NRC-S that have shifted onto a more recently derived helper appear correspondingly released from at least the latter constraint, and their physical clustering suggests that recent tandem duplication has accelerated their diversification, plausibly under pressure to recognize a wider range of effectors, to evade suppression, or to add redundancy to the pathway (Derevnina et al., 2021; Contreras et al., 2023b).

Together these results suggest that the differential tempo of evolution within the NRC network is not incidental but reflects the functional position each receptor occupies. The network confers resistance against an unusually broad range of pathogens, spanning bacteria, fungi, oomycetes, nematodes, and viruses, and individual members such as NRC6 have taken on more specialized tissue- or pathogen-specific roles (Lee et al., 2021). A system in which conserved and rapidly evolving components coexist can retain reliable core signaling while continuing to sample new recognition specificities, and the comparatively simple lettuce network offers a model for how a shift in helper dependency might have licensed that diversification. It is also striking that closely related and functionally connected receptors can differ so markedly in evolutionary rate, echoing the contrast between diverse and conserved NLR types described at the lettuce RGC2 locus (Kuang et al., 2004). Establishing the molecular basis of helper specificity, and of sensor–helper communication more generally, is the natural next step, and would inform both resistance breeding and immune receptor engineering in asterid crops.

Chapter 5

Computational structural modeling of NLR resistosomes reveals structural diversity in plant CC-type NLRs

8 sections·16 figures·15 min read

Overview

In this chapter, I use AlphaFold 3 to address three core questions. First, I test whether computational modeling recapitulates the experimentally resolved NRC2 hexamer, evaluating how predictions hold across different seeds, model versions, and lipid ligands. Second, I benchmark whether model confidence metrics can identify the correct oligomeric state using the established ZAR1 and Sr35 pentamers. Third, I map oligomerization propensity across the NRC helper clade and diverse CC-NLRs across the plant phylogeny.

About this chapter

Part of the work described in this chapter has been published in Madhuprakash et al. (Madhuprakash et al., 2024) and appears here with permission. Cryo-EM structure determination was carried out by Jogi Madhuprakash and Michael Webster. Biochemical and cell death assays were performed by Mauricio Contreras and Jogi Madhuprakash. My contribution comprised the computational structural modeling and the comparative analyses described below.

Chapter 5/Computational structural modeling of NLR resistosomes reveals structural diversity in plant CC-type NLRs

5.1 Introduction

2 min read

The structural basis of NLR-mediated immunity has been transformed over the past few years by a succession of cryo-EM structures of activated receptor complexes. The first of these, the Arabidopsis thaliana CC-NLR AtZAR1, was shown to assemble upon activation into a wheel-shaped pentamer, termed a resistosome, in which the N-terminal α1 helices of the five protomers project outwards to form a funnel that inserts into the plasma membrane and acts as a calcium-permeable channel (Wang et al., 2019b; Wang et al., 2019a; Bi et al., 2021). The wheat CC-NLR Sr35 was subsequently found to adopt the same pentameric architecture (Förderer et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2022), while the TIR-NLR resistosomes ROQ1 and RPP1 assemble as tetramers with an entirely different signaling output (Martin et al., 2020; Ma et al., 2020). For CC-NLRs specifically, the pentamer was regarded as the canonical activated state.

In Chapter 3, we showed that the helper NLR NRC2 rests as a homodimer (Selvaraj et al., 2024). Upon sensor-mediated activation, NRC2 assembles into a hexameric resistosome rather than a pentamer (Madhuprakash et al., 2024). Structural studies on the related helper NRC4 independently confirmed this hexameric architecture (Liu et al., 2023a). Because NRC helpers are activated indirectly by NRC-S that do not incorporate into the resistosome (Contreras et al., 2022; Ahn et al., 2023), these findings overturned the assumption of a universal pentamer. They raised the broader question of how widely oligomeric states vary across plant CC-NLRs, and whether pentamers or hexamers represent the more common active form.

Testing this experimentally across dozens of receptors remains a bottleneck by protein expression, purification, and cryo-EM data collection. Computational structural modeling offers a scalable alternative. AlphaFold 2 established high-throughput and high-quality monomer prediction (Jumper et al., 2021). AlphaFold 2 multimer enabled high-confidence protein complex predictions (Evans et al., 2021), and AlphaFold 3 introduced modeling proteins with ligand, ions, and small molecules (Abramson et al., 2024). Modeling lipids is particularly useful for CC-NLR resistosomes. The CC-NLR resistosome executes cell death via a membrane-inserting funnel and typically mediated by the α1 helix, which is not resolved in most cryo-EM resistosome models.

In this chapter, I use AlphaFold 3 to address three core questions. First, I test whether computational modeling recapitulates the experimentally resolved NRC2 hexamer, evaluating how predictions hold across different seeds, model versions, and lipid ligands. Second, I benchmark whether model confidence metrics can identify the correct oligomeric state using the established ZAR1 and Sr35 pentamers. Third, I map oligomerization propensity across the NRC helper clade and diverse CC-NLRs across the plant phylogeny.

Chapter 5OverviewNext 5.2 AlphaFold 3 predicts a lipid-bound NRC2 resistosome with high confidence

Chapter 5/Computational structural modeling of NLR resistosomes reveals structural diversity in plant CC-type NLRs

5.2 AlphaFold 3 predicts a lipid-bound NRC2 resistosome with high confidence

1 min read

Activated CC-NLR resistosomes insert into the host plasma membrane via a funnel formed by their N-terminal α1 helices. In the NbNRC2 cryo-EM structure, these MADA-containing helices lacked resolved density, leaving the pore unmodeled. I therefore used AlphaFold to predict this missing region and complete the structural model (Abramson et al., 2024).

Using the cryo-EM hexamer as a reference, I compared the performance of AlphaFold 2, AlphaFold 3, and AlphaFold 3 supplemented with 50 oleic acid molecules to simulate the membrane environment (Jumper et al., 2021; Abramson et al., 2024). Given the large size of the NLR oligomer and GPU memory limits, I restricted modeling to the CC-NB-ARC module containing the oligomerization interfaces. I evaluated the resulting predictions using pLDDT, pTM, ipTM, predicted aligned error, minimum per-chain pTM, and chain-pair ipTM.

All three approaches produced high-confidence models with pTM and ipTM values above 0.7, aligning to the experimental structure with RMSD values below 1.8 Å (Figures 5.1A and 5.S1). However, protomer orientations differed fundamentally between versions. In the AlphaFold 2 model, the N-terminal α1 helix pointed inward toward the central pore. In contrast, both AlphaFold 3 models oriented the helix outward, assembling a complete funnel. Adding oleic acid molecules further improved model quality. The α1 helix formed confident contacts with the surrounding lipids, yielding higher local confidence scores than predictions run without lipids (Figures 5.1B and 5.S1). Including a membrane proxy therefore directly guides the outward orientation of the pore-forming helix missing from the cryo-EM map.

I next examined whether the models recovered the experimental oligomerization contacts. Using a 4.5 Å contact cutoff, the AlphaFold 3 model successfully captured most inter-protomer contacts from the cryo-EM structure (Figure 5.1D). Prediction accuracy varied across individual domains. Adjacent CC domains aligned closely with the experimental contacts, whereas adjacent NBD interfaces diverged from the cryo-EM model (Figures 5.1E and 5.S3). AlphaFold 3 thus reliably recovers the overall quaternary architecture, even when specific inter-domain contacts and specific side-chains show local differences.

Chapter 5/Computational structural modeling of NLR resistosomes reveals structural diversity in plant CC-type NLRs

5.3 Model confidence is highest for the hexameric stoichiometry

1 figure·2 min read

After confirming that AlphaFold 3 reliably predicts the hexamer, I tested how varying stoichiometry influences prediction confidence. I modeled NbNRC2 across stoichiometries ranging from four to eight protomers, running ten random seeds per stoichiometry in the presence of 50 oleic acid molecules (Figures 5.1C and 5.S2).

Hexamer models achieved the highest median pTM and ipTM scores, aligning to the experimental structure with RMSD values below 1.8 Å. Pentamers and heptamers scored lower across all metrics, while tetramers and octamers showed lower confidence and higher variance across runs. All oligomeric forms from pentamer to octamer assembled complete funnel structures. In contrast, tetramer runs produced inconsistent assemblies, alternating between closed funnels and split, arc-like incomplete rings (Figure 5.S3A). Model confidence metrics for NbNRC2 therefore clearly distinguish the experimentally determined hexamer from alternative stoichiometries.

These models provide a structural hypothesis for the unresolved N-terminal region. The α1 helices form an outward-facing bundle at the apex of the complex, superimposing onto the protomer core without disrupting the overall fold (Figure 5.S3B). In the hexamer model, these helices frame a central pore lined by a ring of leucine residues at position L126 (Figure 5.S3C). This arrangement provides a concrete model for the channel-forming executioner region.

Previous5.2 AlphaFold 3 predicts a lipid-bound NRC2 resistosome with high confidenceNext 5.4 AtZAR1 and TmSr35 are predicted with higher confidence as pentamers

Chapter 5/Computational structural modeling of NLR resistosomes reveals structural diversity in plant CC-type NLRs

5.4 AtZAR1 and TmSr35 are predicted with higher confidence as pentamers

1 figure·1 min read

I next asked whether AlphaFold 3 could distinguish the pentameric state of AtZAR1 and TmSr35, the two CC-NLRs with known pentameric resistosome structures (Wang et al., 2019a; Förderer et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2022). I modeled the CC-NB-ARC modules of both receptors as pentamers and hexamers. While overall confidence scores were lower than those for NbNRC2, both pentamer models aligned closely with their cryo-EM models, yielding RMSDs of 1.51 Å for Arabidopsis thaliana AtZAR1 and 1.76 Å for TmSr35 (Figure 5.2A). Crucially, both receptors scored higher as pentamers than as hexamers, matching their experimental assemblies (Figure 5.S6).

These benchmarks show that AlphaFold 3 confidence metrics track the correct oligomeric state across all three structurally characterized CC-NLRs. The helper NRC2 scores highest as a hexamer, while the two singletons score highest as pentamers. However, the score differences between stoichiometries remain modest. These metrics should serve as guides to the most probable state rather than definitive proof of assembly, particularly given known limitations of ipTM in evaluating protein interfaces (Dunbrack, 2025; Lin et al., 2025).

Previous5.3 Model confidence is highest for the hexameric stoichiometryNext 5.5 Modeling across the NRC helper clade

Chapter 5/Computational structural modeling of NLR resistosomes reveals structural diversity in plant CC-type NLRs

5.5 Modeling across the NRC helper clade

1 min read

Building on the high-confidence prediction of the NbNRC2 hexamer, I examined structural models of other NRC helpers. I modeled eleven representatives from the major NRC clades described in Chapter 3 as both pentamers and hexamers (Figure 5.S4).

Three of the eleven helpers, specifically SlNRC0, NbNRCX, and NbNRC7a, failed to yield confident models and returned ipTM and pTM scores below 0.6 across both stoichiometries (Figure 5.S5). The remaining eight helpers returned confidence scores of 0.6 or higher in both configurations. For all eleven helpers, hexamer models scored higher than pentamer models, although this difference was often subtle. Every hexamer model except that of NbNRC7a also achieved minimum per-chain pTM scores of 0.7 or higher, a benchmark reached by fewer pentamer models (Figure 5.S5).

The poor prediction scores for NRC0 are particularly notable given its status as the ancestral helper. They align with previous observations of an incomplete N-terminal funnel in modeled NRC0 oligomers (Selvaraj et al., 2024), a feature also observed for the lettuce ortholog LsatNRC0 in Chapter 6. Whether this outcome reflects a genuine divergence in resistosome assembly or simply shallower sequence alignments available for divergent helpers remains an open question.

Previous5.4 AtZAR1 and TmSr35 are predicted with higher confidence as pentamersNext 5.6 CC-NLR resistosomes show a diversity of predicted stoichiometries and N-terminal pores

Chapter 5/Computational structural modeling of NLR resistosomes reveals structural diversity in plant CC-type NLRs

5.6 CC-NLR resistosomes show a diversity of predicted stoichiometries and N-terminal pores

1 min read

Following the benchmark results for NbNRC2, AtZAR1, and TmSr35, I modeled a phylogenetically diverse panel of plant NLRs with unknown resistosome architectures (Figure 5.S7). I tested eight CC-type, six CCG10-type, and two CCR-type NLRs as both pentamers and hexamers to evaluate whether their resistosomes could be predicted with high confidence and to determine their preferred stoichiometry (Figure 5.2B).

Both the CC-type and CCG10-type clades contained representatives of hexameric and pentameric assemblies. Every receptor within the CC-NLR clade modeled with ipTM, pTM, and minimum per-chain pTM values of 0.6 or higher (Figures 5.S8–5.S10 and 5.S14). AtHrt1, AtRpm1, and SlPtr1 yielded higher confidence as hexamers than as pentamers. In contrast, OsPit, TaPm2a, StR3a, SbRpi-blb1, and BvRz2 scored higher in the pentameric form (Figures 5.S8–5.S10). In StR3a and BvRz2, the CC domain and N-terminal α1 helix modeled with lower confidence than in the other resistosomes regardless of stoichiometry (Figures 5.S9 and 5.S10).

The CCG10-NLRs showed a similar split in preferred stoichiometry. AtRPS5 returned higher confidence as a hexamer (Figure 5.S12), whereas CaPvr4, LsatRGC2B, GmRsv3, and CmVat scored higher as pentamers (Figures 5.S11 and 5.S12). AtRPS2 was the sole exception in this group, modeling poorly in both stoichiometries with scores below 0.6 (Figures 5.S11 and 5.S14).

The two CCR-NLRs, NbADR1 and NbNRG1, failed to generate confident models in either configuration and scored below 0.6 throughout (Figures 5.S13 and 5.S14). Even within this low confidence range, both proteins scored slightly higher as pentamers than as hexamers. Because these helper receptors function downstream of TIR-NLR signaling (Castel et al., 2019; Saile et al., 2020; Jacob et al., 2021), these low scores likely reflect current modeling limitations for divergent RPW8-type CC domains rather than an inability to oligomerize.

Previous5.5 Modeling across the NRC helper cladeNext 5.7 Conclusions and discussion

Chapter 5/Computational structural modeling of NLR resistosomes reveals structural diversity in plant CC-type NLRs

5.7 Conclusions and discussion

2 min read

Benchmarked against three experimentally resolved CC-NLR resistosomes, AlphaFold 3 predicted activated NRC hexamers and CC-NLR pentamers with high confidence. The overall fold of the NbNRC2 hexamer was recovered at 1.72 Å RMSD along with key interface residues, while AtZAR1 and TmSr35 pentamers aligned at 1.51 Å and 1.76 Å, respectively. While contacts between adjacent CC domains aligned approximately with experimental interfaces, residues at the NBD–NBD interface showed different side-chain orientations from the cryo-EM structure. The modeling pipeline is therefore best suited to recovering overall resistosome architecture rather than precise atomic contacts across every interface.

The inclusion of membrane lipids proved to be a critical practical factor. Supplying oleic acid molecules enabled high-confidence modeling of the N-terminal funnel. These funnels are frequently unresolved in cryo-EM maps due to non-functional mutations introduced to block cell death or the loss of native lipids during purification. AlphaFold 3 can therefore help fill structural gaps in resistosomes that remain technically challenging to solve experimentally. These findings also demonstrate that providing a lipid proxy substantially improves computational models of membrane-associated complexes.

Model confidence metrics accurately distinguished experimental stoichiometry in all three benchmark cases, favoring a hexamer for NbNRC2 and pentamers for AtZAR1 and TmSr35. This benchmark carries a broader implication. Because published pentameric structures were obtained from proteins expressed in insect cells rather than plants, independent computational support for pentamers suggests that these assemblies are not expression artifacts. Direct purification of these complexes from plant tissue will still be valuable to confirm these states in their native background. While score differences between stoichiometries remain modest, these metrics consistently identify the more probable assembly.

Applied across a broader set of plant NLRs, the pipeline generated confident models for members of both canonical CC and CCG10 clades. Both groups contained receptors that favored pentamers alongside others that favored hexamers, demonstrating that stoichiometry is not fixed within a phylogenetic class. Several CC-NLRs and both CCR-NLRs failed to yield confident assemblies. Within the NRC clade, the three helpers that modeled poorly were SlNRC0, NbNRCX, and NbNRC7a. This is an intriguing pattern, as NRC0 represents the ancestral network helper and NRCX acts as a negative regulator that lacks autonomous cell death activity (Sakai et al., 2024; Adachi et al., 2023a). Building on these observations, we recently developed an expanded computational pipeline to systematically assess oligomeric states across the NRC family. This led to the discovery of an atypical 11-mer resistosome assembly in NRC7 (Toghani et al., 2026b). This result provides further evidence for structural diversity in CC-NLR resistosomes, demonstrating that stoichiometry can vary even among closely related helper paralogs.

The finding that the conserved NB-ARC domain can support multiple oligomeric states highlights unexpected structural flexibility in this family. Further computational and structural work may identify the sequence determinants within the CC and NB-ARC domains that drive the formation of diverse resistosome assemblies. Additionally, AlphaFold 3 provides a platform for hypothesis generation that complements the phylogenomic and functional analyses developed in Chapters 3 and 4.

Chapter 6

Using AI-based modeling to distinguish between Sensor and Helper NLRs

8 sections·13 figures·14 min read

Overview

In this chapter, I use AlphaFold 3 to evaluate the functional roles of genetically linked NLRs computationally. I test whether sensors and helpers exhibit distinct structural signatures in modeled oligomers and examine whether structural modeling provides a more robust classification framework than existing sequence-based criteria.

About this chapter

The work described in this chapter has been published in Toghani et al. (Toghani et al., 2025a) and appears here with permission. The analysis of the lettuce NRC network described at the end of the chapter has been published in Pai et al. (Pai et al., 2026) and likewise appears with permission.

Chapter 6/Using AI-based modeling to distinguish between Sensor and Helper NLRs

6.1 Introduction

2 min read

NLR receptor proteins are encoded in organisms across all kingdoms of life but are especially diversified in plants (Barragan and Weigel, 2021). Receptors carrying a coiled-coil (CC) domain at their N terminus are phylogenetically the most widespread class. Following pathogen recognition, plant CC-NLR receptors oligomerize into pentameric or hexameric pore-like complexes (Wang et al., 2019a; Förderer et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2023a; Madhuprakash et al., 2024). These higher-order complexes, termed resistosomes which are described in Chapter 5, represent the defining feature of NLRs that execute immune responses. Upon activation and complex formation, CC-NLRs translocate to cellular membranes to form pores which allow calcium influx and subsequent cell death (Duggan et al., 2021; Contreras et al., 2022; Ibrahim et al., 2026). The prevailing model indicates that the funnel-shaped resistosome inserts into the membrane to execute cell death via the N-terminal domain (Wang et al., 2019a; Adachi et al., 2019b). The N-terminal α1 helix forms the tip of the funnel and represents a structurally dynamic region that remains difficult to resolve by cryo-EM (Förderer et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2023a; Madhuprakash et al., 2024).

As outlined in Chapters 3 and 4, NLRs can function as singletons, pairs, or networks (Adachi et al., 2019b; Contreras et al., 2023a). While singletons can detect pathogens and execute cell death within a single protein, paired and networked NLR have subfunctionalized into pathogen-detecting sensors and downstream signaling helpers with distinct biochemical roles. Paired NLRs often originate from distinct phylogenetic clades yet function together, which makes it challenging to determine NLR pairs based on sequence phylogeny alone, as compared to NLR networks which often fall into neighboring phylogenetic clades (Kourelis et al., 2021; Contreras et al., 2023a).

Two sequence-based criteria are conventionally used to generally separate sensors from helpers. (I) Sensor and helper pairs often locate within shared genetic clusters. (II) Sensors can carry non-canonical integrated domains (IDs) that act as pathogen baits which are absent from helpers (Białas et al., 2018; Marchal et al., 2018). The presence of an ID therefore provides a useful sequence diagnostic. Additionally, approximately 20% of plant CC-NLRs carry the conserved MADA motif in their N-terminal α1 helix, which this motif has degenerated in some Solanaceous sensor clades (Adachi et al., 2019a). Both criteria remain useful but incomplete, leaving the structural basis underlying sensor and helper specialization unresolved.

AlphaFold 3 might offer a computational strategy to address this gap (Abramson et al., 2024). As shown in Chapter 5, modeling protein complexes with oleic acid molecules simulates the membrane environment and resolves regions that are difficult to capture experimentally, including the N-terminal α1 helix and the resistosome funnel (Madhuprakash et al., 2024). In this chapter, I use AlphaFold 3 to evaluate the functional roles of genetically linked NLRs computationally. I test whether sensors and helpers exhibit distinct structural signatures in modeled oligomers and examine whether structural modeling provides a more robust classification framework than existing sequence-based criteria.

Chapter 6OverviewNext 6.2 Helper NLRs produce higher confidence scores than their paired sensors when modeled as resistosomes

Chapter 6/Using AI-based modeling to distinguish between Sensor and Helper NLRs

6.2 Helper NLRs produce higher confidence scores than their paired sensors when modeled as resistosomes

1 figure·2 min read

I assembled a curated set of CC-NLR pairs comprising experimentally validated pairs in rice (Pikm, Pii, and Pia), their orthologs (PIK5/6-NP, Pi5-3/1, and Pias), and two cloned pairs in barley (RPG5/HvRGA1 and RGH2/3) (Figure 6.S1). Following the approach used in Chapter 5 (Madhuprakash et al., 2024), I extracted the oligomerizing region of each protein from the N terminus through the NB-ARC domain. I then modeled pentameric and hexameric stoichiometries with 50 oleic acid molecules across three random seeds in AlphaFold 3.

Model confidence scores followed a clear, consistent pattern across both pentameric and hexameric configurations. Known helper NLRs yielded higher pTM scores than their respective paired sensor in every case (Figure 6.1a,b, and Figures 6.S2 and 6.S3). When plotting helper against sensor scores, every pair fell above the diagonal line, and ipTM scores showed the same distribution (Figure 6.S4), outlining that this method can be used to distinguish known sensor and helper pairs. For instance, RGH3 reached a pTM of 0.74 compared with 0.31 for its partner RGH2, and Pii-1 reached 0.71 against 0.54 for Pii-2. The score difference was narrowest for RPG5/HvRGA1, where hexameric pTM values were nearly identical (Figure 6.S3). Additionally, pentameric and hexameric scores correlated strongly, as did pTM and ipTM within each stoichiometry (Figure 6.S2), showing that this pattern holds across different scoring metrics, outlining that modeling does not require detailed a priori knowledge of the real oligimeric state.

Upon closer evaluation, the modeled structures showed clear architectural differences between the two classes (Figure 6.1c, and Figures 6.S5 and 6.S6). Helper NLRs assembled into funnel-shaped oligomers that projected their N-terminal α1 helices outward contacting the lipids. In contrast, sensor NLRs failed to form these ordered funnels. This difference aligns with evidence that sensor NLRs cannot trigger immune signaling independently and may have lost the ability to assemble functional resistosomes (Adachi et al., 2019b; Contreras et al., 2022). While sensors occasionally assembled into ring-like structures, these models consistently returned low confidence scores, especially compared to their paired helper (Figure 6.1). AlphaFold 3 predictions therefore reliably distinguish the structural properties of helpers from those of paired sensors.

Previous6.1 IntroductionNext 6.3 Structure-based classification outperforms the MADA motif as a determinant of sensor/helper NLR predictions in paired NLRs

Chapter 6/Using AI-based modeling to distinguish between Sensor and Helper NLRs

6.3 Structure-based classification outperforms the MADA motif as a determinant of sensor/helper NLR predictions in paired NLRs

1 min read

I next tested whether the presence/absence of the MADA motif alone could be used to classify sensors and helpers of paired NLRs in this curated set using the established MADA hidden Markov model (HMM) (Adachi et al., 2019a). Only the helpers of Pikm and PIK5/6-NP paired NLR system contained a motif that exceeded the HMM score cutoff of 10, outlining the presence of a MADA motif. The remaining sensors and helpers lacked detectable motifs. Therefore, the used sequence analysis of the MADA motif only classified two of the eight helpers within the NLR pairs successfully. Because structural modeling separated all eight pairs into non-resistosome sensors and resistosome forming helpers, the structure-based metric provides a substantially more sensitive classification framework than sequence motifs alone.

Previous6.2 Helper NLRs produce higher confidence scores than their paired sensors when modeled as resistosomesNext 6.4 Structure-based classification can be used to predict putative paired NLRs in rice

Chapter 6/Using AI-based modeling to distinguish between Sensor and Helper NLRs

6.4 Structure-based classification can be used to predict putative paired NLRs in rice

1 figure·1 min read

I next extended this structural analysis to predict putative paired NLRs in rice. Taking the rice pan-genome analysis of Stein and colleagues (Stein et al., 2018), I extracted ten rice CC-NLR pairs that are (I) genetically linked in head-to-head orientation, (II) belong to distinct phylogenetic clades, and (III) carry a complete N-terminal CC domain (Figure 6.2a and Figure 6.S1). In five of these ten pairs, one partner carries an ID annotation, identifying it as the putative sensor.

For these five pairs, putative helpers lacking an ID annotation returned higher pTM and ipTM scores than the respective putative sensors, which carry ID annotations (Figure 6.2b,c, and Figures 6.S7–6.S9). These results suggest that AlphaFold 3 can reliably predict sensor and helper identity in uncharacterized pairs, similar to predictions obtained for experimentally validated pairs.

Pair-13 specifically highlights the predictive power of this approach. This pair corresponds to PIK5/6-NP, where PIK5-NP functions as a sensor carrying an integrated domain that escapes detection by InterProScan (Białas et al., 2021; Kourelis et al., 2021). Despite the lack of an annotated ID, AlphaFold 3 prediction correctly identified PIK5-NP as the sensor based on low confidence scores alone. Structural modeling can therefore overcome false negatives in sequence-based domain annotations.

Chapter 6/Using AI-based modeling to distinguish between Sensor and Helper NLRs

6.5 Validation on an experimentally characterized wheat NLR pair

1 min read

After the initial submission of this study, two genetically linked NLR genes in wheat, Pm5e and RXL (Rx-CC-like), arranged head-to-head, were reported to function together as a paired CC-NLR module to confer resistance to powdery mildew (Guo et al., 2025). This pair provides a rigorous test case because Pm5e lacks an annotated ID and both proteins display non-canonical domain architectures, including an atypical CC domain in Pm5e and a truncated NB-ARC domain in RXL.

I tested whether AlphaFold 3 could be used to distinguish between sensor and helper NLR in this newly characterized pair. Consistent with previous predictions, the experimentally validated helper RXL scored higher in both pTM and ipTM across pentameric and hexameric models compared to the validated sensor Pm5e. This result demonstrates that structural modeling successfully predicts helper and sensor pairs that lack distinguishing sequence motifs or canonical domain features.

Previous6.4 Structure-based classification can be used to predict putative paired NLRs in riceNext 6.6 Extension to a dicot NLR network

Chapter 6/Using AI-based modeling to distinguish between Sensor and Helper NLRs

6.6 Extension to a dicot NLR network

1 figure·1 min read

To test whether this structural dichotomy extends beyond monocot pairs into dicot networks, I used AlphaFold 3 to model and predict sensor and helper NLRs in the lettuce NRC network characterized in Chapter 4 (Pai et al., 2026). I modeled each of the two lettuce helpers and the 16 NRC-S as hexamers across five independent replicates with 50 oleic acid molecules. Subsequently, the assemblies were evaluated using pLDDT, pTM, ipTM, and per-chain pTM.

Both helpers assembled into resistosome-like oligomers, though LsatNRC0 failed to form a complete N-terminal funnel, mirroring the behavior of Solanaceous NRC0 in Chapter 5 (Selvaraj et al., 2024). None of the NRC-S across all three phylogenetic groups formed a resistosome assembly (Figure 6.3). In accordance with that, sensor models returned consistently low confidence scores, with high predicted aligned error, pTM and ipTM values below 0.5, and per-chain pTM values below 0.7 (Figure 6.S10). In contrast, the helpers scored above 0.5 for both pTM and ipTM in every replicate, with per-chain pTM averaging 0.75 (Figure 6.3).

The structural distinction observed in monocot pairs therefore extends to dicot networks where NRC-S lack integrated domains. Importantly, cell death assays in Chapter 4 experimentally validated these functional relationships. In those assays, autoactive sensor mutants did not trigger cell death alone, but activated wild-type helpers to execute cell death. AlphaFold 3 predictions are able to directly capture this functional asymmetry.

Chapter 6/Using AI-based modeling to distinguish between Sensor and Helper NLRs

6.7 Conclusions and discussion

2 min read

The lower confidence scores for oligomeric resistosome predictions observed for sensor and higher scores observed for helper NLRs within NLR pairs align with evolutionary models of NLR subfunctionalization (Adachi et al., 2019b). In this model, ancestral singletons capable of both perception and execution subfunctionalized into specialized sensors and helpers (Adachi et al., 2019b; Contreras et al., 2023a). Sensors lost execution activity while helpers lost pathogen detection. Because assembling a funnel-shaped resistosome, followed by integration into the membrane to form a channel is required to trigger cell death, the retention of stable resistosome funnels in helpers and their loss in sensors structurally further supports this division of labor. Given that AlphaFold 3 failed to model these properties for sensor NLRs, these findings further suggest that sensor NLRs have lost the intrinsic capacity to assemble into autonomous resistosomes, consistent with experimental observations for the Solanaceous sensor Rx (Contreras et al., 2022).

Notably, the helpers Pia-1, Pias-1, and RGH3 lack detectable MADA motifs yet assembled outward-facing funnels in the AlphaFold models, when modeled as penta- or hexamers. This raises the possibility that alternative sequence patterns drive membrane insertion in these non-MADA helpers. Structural determination by cryo-EM combined with large-scale modeling will be required to define the motifs driving funnel formation in these divergent helpers.

This computational framework has three primary limitations. First, these generated models focus exclusively on active resistosome assemblies and do not evaluate resting states, which range from monomers and homodimers to higher-order oligomers as shown in Chapter 3 (Wang et al., 2019a; Selvaraj et al., 2024). Second, unlike helper NLRs we still do not have any structural evidence for how sensor NLRs, especially NRC-S, look like in their resting or activated states. Third, these simulations test homo-oligomers and do not assess whether paired NLRs assemble into hetero-complexes. The wheat pair RXL/Pm5e highlights this consideration, as these proteins preferentially form hetero-complexes (Guo et al., 2025) that homo-oligomeric modeling cannot capture.

The primary aim of this work was to evaluate AlphaFold as a predictive tool for classifying NLRs into functional sensors and helpers, which are highly diverse, often number in the hundreds per plant genome, and collectively account for approximately 1% of all plant genes, as quantified in Chapter 2 (Toghani and Kamoun, 2024). Combined with the evolutionary analyses in Chapters 3 and 4 and the structural modeling in Chapter 5, these results show that structural prediction can characterize NLR function within genetically paired NLR clusters and prioritize candidate sensor and helper genes for experimental validation. Such structural insights will help elucidate how the distinct architectures of sensors and helpers drive their functional specialization. However, the molecular determinants of sensor NLR emergence remains elusive. Moreover, given the reliance of AlphaFold 3 on multiple sequence alignments and evolutionary information, the differences in the oligomer prediction of sensor and helper NLRs suggests that AlphaFold 3 is detecting a signal in the amino acid sequence of these proteins. This may help uncover the molecular determinants of sensor-NLR evolution in future studies.

Chapter 7

General Discussion

5 sections·1 figure·8 min read

Overview

The evolution of plant NLR immune receptors is most often framed as an arms race with pathogen effectors. Pathogens deploy effectors, receptors evolve recognition, pathogens mutate to evade detection, and the cycle repeats. This dynamic is well documented, and its molecular signature appears throughout the sensor datasets analyzed in this thesis. Yet the arms-race model primarily explains the recognition surfaces of sensor and singleton NLRs. It reveals little about the rest of the protein, and it does not explain why helper NLRs, which do not recognize pathogen effectors directly, evolve at distinct rates. This thesis investigated the selective pressures that act on NLRs from within the immune receptor network.

Three core conclusions emerge from this work. First, the evolutionary rate of an NLR reflects partner compatibility rather than functional output alone. Second, NLR sequence evolution proceeds under distinct regimes that act on separate domains of the protein. Third, sensor subfunctionalization involves the loss of autonomous oligomerization, which potentially explains why structural modeling can distinguish sensors from helpers where sequence motifs fail (Figure 7.1).

Chapter 7/General Discussion

7.1 Diversification structured by internal partner compatibility

2 min read

Two findings in this thesis indicate that sequence variation is structured by internal partner compatibility rather than by direct pathogen pressure. In lettuce, the rate of sensor diversification correlated with helper dependency, forming a spectrum from receptors dependent on the ancestral NRC0 to those signaling through the lineage-specific derived helper Ast-LsatNRC1 (Chapter 4). Within the Solanaceae NRC helper clade, the interfaces mediating helper homodimerization diverged between clades while remaining conserved within them (Chapter 3).

Consequently, the classification of an NLR as a sensor or a helper does not fully define the selective pressure acting on it. Instead, evolutionary constraint depends on the position of the receptor within the network, reflecting both the number of its interacting partners and their evolutionary conservation. A helper downstream of multiple sensors and a sensor dependent on an ancestral helper both face evolutionary constraint that does not stem directly from pathogen exposure (Figure 7.1).

This model also refines the classic view of sensor–helper subfunctionalization. Specialization is usually described as relaxed evolutionary pressure on individual receptors that frees sensors to diversify (Adachi et al., 2019b). The results presented here suggest that subfunctionalization can redistribute constraint across the network rather than remove it. Sensors lost the ability to execute cell death but acquired the requirement to signal through a cognate helper. Conversely, helpers were released from pathogen detection but must maintain compatibility with an expanding repertoire of upstream sensors.

One caveat should be noted. The correlation between helper dependency and sensor diversification observed in Chapter 4 is consistent with two alternative mechanisms that current data cannot separate. Sensors dependent on the ancestral NRC0 may be constrained by the need to maintain helper compatibility, or by the host targets they monitor, particularly if they guard conserved host components in a manner analogous to the ZAR1–ZRK system (Adachi et al., 2023b). Nevertheless, these sensors often show signs of diversification in regions not typically implicated in effector recognition, such as the coiled-coil (CC) domain. This could be interpreted as a sign of relaxed selection following subfunctionalization within these sensors. Distinguishing between these possibilities requires identifying receptors that have switched helper dependency while retaining effector recognition specificity. Testing such natural or engineered variants will be essential to establish a direct causal mechanism.

Chapter 7OverviewNext 7.2 Selection pressures beyond R-AVR co-evolution

Chapter 7/General Discussion

7.2 Selection pressures beyond R-AVR co-evolution

2 min read

By studying multiple NRC helpers and their sensors across this thesis, I found several distinct patterns of diversification. The most rapidly evolving lettuce sensors carry sites under positive selection concentrated on the concave face of the LRR, the surface implicated in effector binding, as described for highly variable receptors such as RPP1 (Prigozhin and Krasileva, 2021). The most constrained lettuce sensors carry variable sites in the CC domain and the N-terminal portion of the LRR rather than at the concave LRR surface implicated in recognition (Chapter 4). Helper NLRs, in contrast, show a different pattern. The homodimerization interfaces of the NRC helpers are less conserved than the P-loop and MHD motifs across the clade, yet well conserved within individual clades, with polymorphisms unique to each (Chapter 3).

Under the classical R-AVR co-evolution model, sustained diversification is favored because it enables novel recognition of effectors by the receptor, or evasion of recognition by the effector. As discussed throughout this thesis, this pattern is usually observed at recognition interfaces such as the concave side of the LRR domain or the exposed surfaces of Solanaceous or integrated domains. However, I detected two additional patterns of diversification, one in NRC helpers and one in their sensors. In NRC helpers, stretches in the CC, NB-ARC, and LRR domains mediate homodimerization and, at least in tomato NRC2, homotetramerization of the helpers in their resting state (Selvaraj et al., 2024; Ma et al., 2024). Consistent with biochemical, microscopy, and genetic data, I hypothesized that the diversification of these stretches leads to insulation of the helper signaling pathways, which may contribute to the fine-tuning and robustness of the network. My analysis of NRC helpers is consistent with this model, which points to a selection pressure that acts within the network, independent of the classical R-AVR co-evolution paradigm that mostly applies to sensor NLRs. Helper NLRs have also been reported to co-evolve directly with pathogen effectors, not for recognition, but to evade suppression (Sugihara et al., 2025). This model has been dubbed “Gene-for-Gene 2.0” (Contreras, 2023; Sugihara et al., 2025).

Moreover, I found that not all sensor NLRs evolve in the same way. While the main evolutionary pressure considered for sensor NLRs relates to effector recognition, NRC0-dependent sensors showed little or no diversification on the concave side of their LRR domain. Instead, their diversified regions were located in the CC domain. Whether these patterns relate to sensor–helper communication, or whether these sensors function differently from others, remains an open question.

Taken together, the conclusions of this thesis expand these evolutionary models into a multi-layered framework in which effector recognition, evasion of suppression, receptor–receptor communication, and the maintenance of robust signaling all shape NLR evolution (Figure 7.1).

Previous7.1 Diversification structured by internal partner compatibilityNext 7.3 Subfunctionalization and the loss of the ability to oligomerize

Chapter 7/General Discussion

7.3 Subfunctionalization and the loss of the ability to oligomerize

1 min read

The degeneration of N-terminal motifs in sensor NLRs is conventionally explained by a use-it-or-lose-it model, in which sensors that rely on helpers for cell death lost the MADA motif (Adachi et al., 2019a). It has also been shown that NRC-dependent sensor NLRs do not oligomerize or become part of the helper resistosome (Contreras et al., 2022; Ahn et al., 2023). However, the loss of oligomerization cannot be attributed only to the loss of the MADA motif, because the motif is also absent from the helpers of many sensor–helper pairs (Chapter 6). To address this limitation, I used AlphaFold 3 modeling of NLR homo-oligomeric resistosomes to assess whether AlphaFold 3 can distinguish between sensor and helper NLRs. Based on confidence metrics alone, sensor NLRs were generally modeled with lower confidence than their helper counterparts across several sensor–helper systems, including monocot paired NLRs and the superasterid NRC network. From these data, I concluded that the loss of oligomerization is likely a product of sensor NLR subfunctionalization. This suggests that AlphaFold 3 detects a feature of sensor sequences that prevents them from being modeled with high confidence as resistosome-like oligomers. This feature likely resides within the CC or NB-ARC domains of sensor NLRs, where the oligomerization interfaces have undergone regressive evolution and degenerated.

However, one caveat is that the mechanism of action of many sensor–helper pairs, particularly the monocot paired NLRs, is still unknown (Pai et al., 2025b). Although NRC-dependent sensors are known to activate their helpers transiently, the activation mechanism may differ for other sensor–helper pairs. For instance, homo-oligomer modeling is inconclusive for sensor–helper pairs that may form a hetero-oligomeric resistosome complex (Guo et al., 2025).

Furthermore, poor modeling results do not necessarily define an NLR as a sensor. Poor modeling confidence can also point to neofunctionalization, as in NRCX (Adachi et al., 2023a), or to the formation of atypical assemblies, as in NRC7 (Toghani et al., 2026b). The modeling outcome should therefore be interpreted in its biological context and treated as a hypothesis.

Previous7.2 Selection pressures beyond R-AVR co-evolutionNext 7.4 How many protomers in a resistosome?

Chapter 7/General Discussion

7.4 How many protomers in a resistosome?

2 min read

The computational modeling in Chapter 5 preceded the public release of NRC hexamer structures and was prompted by the determination of the NbNRC2 hexamer in our laboratory. Using AlphaFold 3, I showed that structural modeling can predict resistosome assemblies across diverse CC-type NLRs and reconstruct unresolved regions such as the membrane-inserting N-terminal α1 helix. In addition, AlphaFold 3 confidence metrics distinguished the correct oligomeric stoichiometry for the NbNRC2, AtZAR1, and TmSr35 resistosomes, although the score differences between stoichiometries were modest.

At the start of this project, the pentameric resistosome was regarded as the canonical activated state of plant CC-NLRs. Subsequent work revealed that NRC helpers assemble as hexamers (Liu et al., 2023a; Madhuprakash et al., 2024). Recent structural studies further showed that the wheat CCG10-NLR WAI3 and Arabidopsis thaliana RPS2 form octamers (Guo et al., 2026). Most recently, our analysis revealed that the helper NRC7 assembles into an atypical 11-mer resistosome (Toghani et al., 2026b). Together, these discoveries show that plant CC-type NLRs form assemblies of five, six, eight, and eleven protomers, which raises the question of why NLRs adopt distinct oligomeric states.

Although the NB-ARC domain is one of the most conserved modules in plant NLRs, it supports assemblies ranging from four protomers in TIR-NLR resistosomes (Ma et al., 2020; Martin et al., 2020) to eleven in NRC7. The structural determinants that govern stoichiometry remain unresolved. One possibility is that the NB-ARC domain provides a flexible structural scaffold, while the N-terminal executioner domain or the C-terminal LRR dictates the final number of protomers. For example, the loss of the canonical EDVID motif has been proposed to drive the divergent coiled-coil packing observed in octameric CCG10-NLRs (Sulkowski et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2026).

The biological significance of this architectural variation is also unclear. In structurally resolved resistosomes, higher protomer counts expand the pore diameter. While known resistosomes trigger calcium influx and cell death upon activation, a larger pore may allow larger molecules to cross the host membrane. Furthermore, consistent with the sequence diversification of N-terminal executioner domains, activated NLRs can target distinct cellular compartments, including chloroplasts (Ibrahim et al., 2026) and vacuoles (Sunil et al., 2024). As in animal innate immunity, plant NLR signaling may encompass diverse execution mechanisms that converge on programmed cell death. The selective pressures that drive the evolution of distinct stoichiometries, and their precise physiological outputs, are yet to be determined.

Previous7.3 Subfunctionalization and the loss of the ability to oligomerizeNext 7.5 Outlook

Chapter 7/General Discussion

7.5 Outlook

1 min read

In this thesis, I investigated NLR biology from evolutionary and structural perspectives. In addition to classical arms-race dynamics with pathogens, these receptors experience distinct selective pressures that insulate and optimize immune signaling networks (Figure 7.1). Helper NLRs appear to evolve to keep their activation pathways separate and to prevent hetero-association with paralogs. Furthermore, while sensor NLRs diversify more rapidly than helpers overall, their evolutionary rates vary with their helper dependency and their potential recognition targets.

Using computational modeling, I showed that AlphaFold 3 generates high-confidence resistosome models that can accelerate the structural biology of plant NLRs. This is particularly useful given the sequence diversity and stoichiometric variation of NLR complexes across green plants. More broadly, structural modeling can distinguish helpers from sensors based on their predicted capacity to assemble into homo-oligomers. This structural criterion complements sequence-based annotation pipelines and could help predict sensor–helper relationships and map genetic dependencies from genomic datasets, with potential applications in crop breeding.

Throughout this thesis, I integrated phylogenomics, computational structural biology, and in planta functional assays to generate mechanistic hypotheses and test evolutionary principles. Combining AI-guided workflows with targeted functional experiments should speed up the study of immune receptor evolution and support the rational engineering of durable disease resistance.

Chapter 2: Curation of harmonized plant NLRome datasets on multiple taxonomic resolutions

1 min read

Genome assemblies and annotationNLR annotationAssessment of annotation completeness

Genome assemblies and annotation

High-quality publicly available genome assemblies were compiled for each of the three datasets. For the 180 RefSeq reference plant proteomes, annotated proteomes were downloaded directly from the NCBI RefSeq database (Pruitt et al., 2007), and no de novo gene prediction was performed. For the 230 superasterid and 346 Solanaceae genome collections, harmonized annotations were generated de novo. Helixer v0.3.2 (Stiehler et al., 2021; Holst et al., 2023) was run using Singularity on the genome FASTA files with the option –lineage land_plant, which applies the default land-plant model (land_plant_v0.3_a_0080.h5). Coding sequences (CDS) and protein FASTA files were extracted from the resulting GFF files using GffRead v0.12.7 (Pertea and Pertea, 2020) with the -x and -y options, respectively.

NLR annotation

The extracted protein sequences were analyzed using NLRtracker (Kourelis et al., 2021), which integrates InterProScan for domain identification (Blum et al., 2025), to detect NLR and NLR-associated sequences. NLRs were defined according to the NLR definition established for the RefPlantNLR dataset (Kourelis et al., 2021).

Assessment of annotation completeness

BUSCO scores were generated using BUSCO v5.5.0 with the options -m protein –lineage_dataset viridiplantae_odb10 for the superasterid dataset, and BUSCO v6.0.0 with -m protein –lineage_dataset solanales_odb12 for the Solanaceae dataset (Manni et al., 2021). For the RefSeq dataset, annotation BUSCO scores provided by NCBI were used where available. Genome annotations were organized by phylogenetic order following the APG IV classification (The Angiosperm Phylogeny Group, 2016). Summary statistics were computed and plotted in Python; the scripts and source data are archived with the thesis.

Phylogenetic analyses of the NRC networkMapping of dimerization stretches and conserved motifsShannon entropy analysisIdentification of clade-unique residuesExtraction of CC domains and N-terminal sequencesTransient protein expression and cell death assays

Phylogenetic analyses of the NRC network

NLRtracker (Kourelis et al., 2021) output from 123 genome assemblies representing 38 species across 4 genera of the Solanaceae (Sugihara et al., 2023) was imported into R, from which 66,451 full-length NLR sequences were extracted. Of these, the 23,872 sequences with domain architectures of “CNL” or “CN” as determined by NLRtracker were retained, and their NB-ARC domains extracted. The NB-ARC sequences of RefPlantNLR (Kourelis et al., 2021), together with tomato (Wu et al., 2017) and pepper (Lee et al., 2021) NRC helpers, were added to this set. Using the NB-ARC domain boundaries reported by NLRtracker, only sequences with NB-ARC domains between 300 and 400 amino acids in length were kept, so that truncated or unusually long sequences were discarded. This left 19,760 sequences, which were aligned with MAFFT v7.505 [–anysymbol] (Katoh and Standley, 2013) and used to generate a phylogenetic tree with FastTree v2.1.11 [-lg] (Price et al., 2010).

The NRC network superclade, comprising 10,665 sequences including both helpers and sensors, was extracted from the CC-NLR tree by selecting the major branch containing both the reference NRC helpers and sensors, using Dendroscope v3.8.10 (Huson and Scornavacca, 2012). These sequences were realigned and used to build a new tree, from which the NRC helper clade was extracted in the same way. The resulting 1,796 NRC helper sequences, excluding the reference sequences, were deduplicated with CD-HIT v4.8.1 [-c 1.00] (Fu et al., 2012). Deduplication was performed to capture the greatest diversity without biasing the analysis through over-represented sequences.

The deduplicated sequences were then filtered by length, retaining only those between 750 and 950 amino acids, which left 993 sequences. This threshold was chosen on the basis of the length distribution of the NRC helper set and the lengths of the reference NRC sequences. The NB-ARC domains of these 993 sequences were combined with the length-filtered NB-ARCs (300–400 amino acids) of reference NRC helpers from N. benthamiana (16 sequences), tomato (13), pepper (10), potato (42), and RefPlantNLR (14), giving 1,088 sequences in total, and aligned with MAFFT. The alignment was used to construct a further tree with FastTree, from which NRC helper subclades were delimited on the basis of reference NRCs falling within well-supported major branches. Sequences falling outside or between major clades were not assigned to a subclade. Clades were extracted with Dendroscope as before.

The full set of 1,092 NRC sequences comprises the 993 filtered full-length sequences together with the unfiltered reference sequences from N. benthamiana (16), tomato (13), pepper (14), potato (42), and RefPlantNLR (14). These were aligned with MAFFT [–localpair] in order to locate the dimerization stretches across all NRC helpers, and the alignment was trimmed with ClipKIT v2.0.1 [-m gappy] to remove sites with 90% gaps (Steenwyk et al., 2020).

Mapping of dimerization stretches and conserved motifs

The dimerization stretches and conserved sequence motifs were mapped onto the alignment of all NRC helpers on the basis of NbNRC2 and the NLRtracker output, and extracted using custom R scripts. Sequence logo plots for the stretches and motifs were generated with the ggseqlogo R package (Wagih, 2017).

Shannon entropy analysis

Shannon entropy values were calculated for all NRC helpers together and for each NRC clade separately, using the entropy R package (Hausser and Strimmer, 2009). Entropy ranges from zero for a fully conserved position to a maximum of 4.32 (log220) where all 20 amino acids occur with equal frequency. A threshold of 1.5 was used to identify highly variable positions, consistent with previous NLR studies (Prigozhin and Krasileva, 2021).

Identification of clade-unique residues

To identify residues unique to individual NRC clades, the relative amino acid ratio was calculated among the NRC2, NRC3, NRC4a, NRC4b, and NRC4other clades. Sequences were first divided into query and subject groups. Using the trimmed alignment of NRC helpers, the amino acid frequency at each position was calculated for both groups, and the frequency in the query group divided by that in the subject group at the same position. Only positions at which an amino acid frequency exceeded 80% within the query group were retained, and positions with a relative amino acid ratio greater than 50 were regarded as unique to the query clade.

Extraction of CC domains and N-terminal sequences

From the same NLRtracker output, the CC domain of each NLR was extracted from the start of the sequence to the beginning of the NB-ARC domain as determined by NLRtracker. The CC domain sequences were used for motif analysis with MEME (Bailey et al., 2015). To extract the N-terminal α1 helix, the CC domain sequences were first processed with NetSurfP-3.0 (Høie et al., 2022) to determine helix boundaries; the α1 helix was then extracted using a custom R script and used for clustering. Unbiased clustering of the N-terminal sequences was performed with MCL (Van Dongen, 2008), and the resulting clusters were mapped onto the NRC helper phylogeny. MADA motifs were identified using the MADA hidden Markov model (Adachi et al., 2019a) with HMMER (Eddy, 2011).

Transient protein expression and cell death assays

Proteins of interest were transiently expressed in N. benthamiana following previously described methods (Wu et al., 2017). In brief, leaves of 4–5-week-old plants were infiltrated with suspensions of Agrobacterium tumefaciens GV3101 pMP90 transformed with the relevant expression vectors. The final OD600 of all suspensions was adjusted in infiltration buffer (10 mM MES, 10 mM MgCl2, and 150 μM acetosyringone, pH 5.6), and an OD600 of 0.3 was used for each construct. Autoactive variants were generated by introducing a D-to-V substitution within the MHD motif (Adachi et al., 2019a). Assays were performed in wild-type and in nrc2/3/4 CRISPR knockout N. benthamiana lines (Wu et al., 2017).

Chapter 4: Contrasting patterns of evolution in sensor and helper NLRs

5 min read

Extraction of NRC network sequencesPhylogenetic and gene distance analysesLinking previous lettuce NLRome classifications to the new annotationCloning, agroinfiltration, and cell death assaysSequence polymorphism and selection analyses

Extraction of NRC network sequences

A total of 29,261 NLRs were compiled from the NLRtracker output of 39 Solanales and 29 Asterales de novo annotated high-quality genome assemblies obtained from NCBI, together with a chromosome-level Solanum melongena assembly from the GWH Genome Warehouse. Annotation followed the Helixer-based workflow described for Chapter 2. On the basis of the simplified NLRtracker domain annotation, only NLRs with the domain architectures “CNL”, “CNLO”, “CN”, “OCNL”, “CONL”, “NL”, “NLO”, “ONL”, “BCNL”, “BNL”, “BCN”, “BCCNL”, “BNLO”, “BOCNL”, “RNL”, “TN”, “TNL”, “TNLO”, and “TNLJ” were retained, leaving 25,042 sequences. These were deduplicated with a custom R script removing redundancy at 100% sequence identity, giving 24,518 non-redundant sequences. Finally, entries whose NB-ARC domain was shorter than 250 or longer than 400 amino acids were removed, yielding the 21,232 sequences used for phylogenetic analysis.

To construct a phylogenetic tree of the extracted NLRs, the NB-ARC domain sequences were aligned together with the RefPlantNLR NB-ARCs using FAMSA v2.2.2 with default options (Deorowicz et al., 2016), and the alignment used to build a tree with FastTree v2.1.11 [-lg] (Price et al., 2010; Kourelis et al., 2021). The NRC network, together with CcRPP1 and its orthologs, was extracted as a well-supported branch containing both NRC helpers and sensors identified by reference sequences. The NB-ARC domains of the extracted sequences were aligned with MAFFT v7.525 (Katoh and Standley, 2013) and used to construct a new tree as before, which was rooted on the CcRPP1 phylogroup.

Phylogenetic and gene distance analyses

Plant taxonomy trees and taxon divergence times were obtained from the TimeTree 5 database (Kumar et al., 2022). From the dataset, 122 NRC sequences including helpers and sensors from Lactuca sativa, L. saligna, L. virosa, Cichorium intybus, Helianthus annuus, Chrysanthemum lavandulifolium, Cynara cardunculus, and Codonopsis lanceolata were extracted on the basis of phylogeny. Their NB-ARC sequences were aligned with AtZAR1, NbZAR1, NbNRC2, and SlNRC0 as references using MAFFT v7.525 [–anysymbol], and FastTree v2.1.11 [-lg] used to generate the tree of the NRC network in these species. IQ-TREE v2.3.0 [-B 1000 -m MFP] (Minh et al., 2020) was then used to generate a phylogenetic tree of the 40 NRC network sequences of the Lactuca genus. The resulting tree was divided into helpers and sensor groups 1, 2, and 3 on the basis of branch lengths and reference sequences.

To determine the physical location of genes on the chromosomes, the GFF output from Helixer was first simplified with GffRead using default options (Pertea and Pertea, 2020) and then imported into R with the rtracklayer package (Lawrence et al., 2009). Physical distances between genes were calculated with a custom R script, and gene coordinates exported for visualization on chromosomes using the MG2C online tool (Chao et al., 2021). The output was then arranged manually.

Linking previous lettuce NLRome classifications to the new annotation

Lettuce NLRome identifiers from Christopoulou and colleagues (Christopoulou et al., 2015) and the Lettuce V8 genome assembly from Phytozome 13 (Goodstein et al., 2012) were retrieved. BLASTP, as part of BLAST+ v2.16.0 (Camacho et al., 2009), was used to identify the gene identifiers in the Phytozome 13 annotation corresponding to the new Helixer annotation. The BLAST output was processed in R, and gene coordinates, major resistance locus information, and RGC group assignments retrieved for the new annotation. Corresponding genes between the two annotations were identified from BLAST hits with greater than 98% sequence identity and bit scores above 1500. The same approach was used to retrieve corresponding sequences from the RefSeq reference annotation of Lsat_Salinas_v11 (GCF_002870075.4).

Cloning, agroinfiltration, and cell death assays

The NRC sequences used in the cell death assays were originally retrieved from the Phytozome 13 annotation and cross-checked against the Helixer annotation, with two sequences absent from the latter. Annotated genes were cloned using the Golden Gate Modular Cloning (MoClo) kit and the MoClo Plant Parts kit. In brief, coding sequences were synthesized by GENEWIZ as Golden Gate Level 0 pICH41155 modules and subsequently transferred into the binary vector pICH86988 by BsaI digestion; native BsaI sites in the original sequences were domesticated as required. In addition to wild-type clones, a D-to-V substitution within the MHD motif was introduced to generate autoactive versions of the lettuce NRCs (Adachi et al., 2019a). Verified clones were transformed into A. tumefaciens strain GV3101 pMP90 for ectopic expression in N. benthamiana.

For the cell death assays, wild-type and nrc2/3/4 N. benthamiana plants were grown in a controlled environment chamber at 22–25C with a 16-hour photoperiod and 45%/65% relative humidity during the light and dark cycles respectively, at a light intensity of approximately 200 μmol m−2 s−1. Four- to five-week-old plants were used for agroinfiltration following previously described methods. The final OD600 of all Agrobacterium suspensions was adjusted to 0.5 in infiltration buffer (10 mM MES, 10 mM MgCl2, and 150 μM acetosyringone, pH 5.6), for both individual expression and co-expression of the NRC helpers and sensors of interest. Cell death phenotypes were imaged 4–5 days post-agroinfiltration.

Sequence polymorphism and selection analyses

Nucleotide sequences of the NRC genes were obtained with a custom Python script from a compiled CDS file of the annotated genomes. Codon-based nucleotide alignments were generated for each NRC helper and sensor phylogroup using MACSE v2.07 [-prog alignSequences -seq] (Ranwez et al., 2018). Positive selection tests were conducted on the resulting alignments using CodeML in PAML v4.10.7 (Yang, 1997). For each phylogroup (helpers and sensor groups 1, 2, and 3), two site models were evaluated: M8a (beta + ω = 1) and M8 (beta + ω). Likelihood ratio tests (2ΔL = 2(lnLalternative−lnLnull)) were performed comparing M8a against M8 (df  = 1; χ2 critical value 6.63 at the 1% significance level). Sites under positive selection were identified with the Bayes Empirical Bayes method (Yang, 2005) under the M8 model, with posterior probabilities greater than 0.95, and the more stringent 0.99, taken to indicate strong support.

To compare average selective pressure across the NRC subclades, PAML branch model 2 was run in CodeML (model = 2, NSsites = 0, CodonFreq = 2), assigning each of the four subclades its own ω parameter via $1–$4 labels placed at the most recent common ancestor of each subclade in the rooted tree. This four-ratio model was tested against the one-ratio model (M0; model = 0) by likelihood ratio test (df  = 4). Per-subclade tree dS lengths were obtained by summing the M0 branch-level dS estimates over the stem and internal branches of each subclade. The free-ratio model (M1; model = 1) was also run for exploratory visualization of branch-level heterogeneity and is not used for hypothesis testing; in this model, branches with ω ≥ 10 reflect low synonymous substitution rates (dS  ≈ 0) and are flagged as ambiguous rather than as evidence of positive selection.

Pairwise nonsynonymous (dN) and synonymous (dS) substitution rates were estimated for full-length sequences and for the individual CC, NB-ARC, and LRR domains within each phylogroup using the Nei and Gojobori method (Nei and Gojobori, 1986). These rates were extracted from the 2NG.dN and 2NG.dS outputs of CodeML with a custom R script. Figures were generated with the ggplot2 R package (Wickham, 2016).

Chapter 8/Materials and Methods

Chapter 5: Computational structural modeling of NLR resistosomes reveals structural diversity in plant CC-type NLRs

1 min read

Structural modeling and processing

Structural modeling and processing

ColabFold v1.5.5 (Mirdita et al., 2022; Jumper et al., 2021) was used to model the NbNRC2 CC-NB-ARC region. The AlphaFold 3 web server (Abramson et al., 2024) was used to model the CC-NB-ARC domains of 11 NRC helpers, 10 CC-NLRs, 6 CCG10-NLRs, and 2 CCR-NLRs, in each case with 50 oleic acid molecules as a proxy for the plasma membrane. The default seed was set to 1; the NbNRC4c and NbNRG1 hexamers were modeled with seed 11. To assess reproducibility of the NbNRC2 oligomers, nine additional models were generated with randomized seed values in addition to the default seed. From each modeling run only the top-ranked model (model_0) was retained and processed.

The ipTM, pTM, chain-pair ipTM, and minimum per-chain pTM values were extracted from the AlphaFold 3 JSON metadata files using custom scripts and plotted in R. The AlphaFold 3 models corresponding to the cryo-EM structures of NbNRC2 (PDB 9FP6), AtZAR1 (6J5T), and TmSr35 (7XE0) were aligned to those structures using the matchmaker function of ChimeraX with default options (Pettersen et al., 2021). Contact points were extracted from the AlphaFold structures using the ChimeraX alphafold contacts command with a distance cut-off of 4.5 Å. All structures were visualized in ChimeraX and assembled manually.
