Chapter 8/Materials and Methods

Chapter 6: Using AI-based modeling to distinguish between Sensor and Helper NLRs

2 min read

NLR annotationCuration of NLR sequencesAlphaFold 3 predictionStatistical analysis and phylogenetics

NLR annotation

NLRs were annotated using NLRtracker v1.0.3 (Kourelis et al., 2021) and InterProScan v5.67-99.0 (Blum et al., 2025). InterProScan did not annotate an integrated domain in PIK5-NP, contrary to a previous report (Kourelis et al., 2021); the domain architecture of PIK5-NP was therefore manually changed from “CNL” to “CONL”, since it contains an HMA domain between the NB-ARC and LRR domains (Białas et al., 2021). Domain architectures were visualized with refplantnlR. MADA motifs were analyzed using the hidden Markov model of Adachi and colleagues (Adachi et al., 2019a) together with HMMER v3.4 (Eddy, 2011) with the –max option.

Curation of NLR sequences

The sequences of the curated NLR pairs were obtained either from RefPlantNLR (Kourelis et al., 2021) or from NCBI. For the NLR pairs described by Stein and colleagues (Stein et al., 2018), the protein sequences of Oryza sativa cv. Nipponbare were downloaded from the accompanying data release. From those data, NLR pairs that are genetically linked in head-to-head orientation and belong to distinct phylogenetic clades were extracted. Using DIAMOND BLASTP v2.1.9 (Buchfink et al., 2015), the corresponding NLR sequences were identified in the NCBI RefSeq annotation of the rice cultivar Nipponbare genome (GCF_034140825.1). The best-hit sequences were retained and confirmed to be genetically linked in a head-to-head orientation. On the basis of the NLRtracker output, only the CC-NLR pairs carrying a full N-terminal CC domain were kept. Pair-05, Pair-13, and the sensor of Pair-14 correspond to Pia, PIK5/6-NP, and Pi-ta, respectively.

AlphaFold 3 prediction

Using the NLRtracker output, the amino acid sequences from the N terminus to the end of the NB-ARC domain were extracted. These were modeled with the AlphaFold 3 web server (Abramson et al., 2024) in both pentameric and hexameric configurations, in each case with 50 oleic acid molecules and using three different seed values (1, 2, and 3). For the wheat helper RXL, the full-length amino acid sequence was used as input owing to its atypical domain architecture (Guo et al., 2025). For the NLR pairs described by Stein and colleagues (Stein et al., 2018), the pTM scores of the pentameric and hexameric configurations were averaged, and the members of each pair assigned as putative helpers or sensors according to whether their score was the higher or the lower of the two.

For the lettuce NRC network, the two helpers and 16 sensors were modeled as hexamers with 50 oleic acid molecules. The first model of each sequence was generated with seed 1 and four further replicates with random seeds. Model confidence values and metadata were processed and plotted in R.

Statistical analysis and phylogenetics

Welch’s t-test was performed using the ttest_ind function of the SciPy Python library with the option equal_var = False. The tree of monocot paired NLRs was built using RefPlantNLR (Kourelis et al., 2021) together with a set of 4,936 NLR proteins from the NLRtracker output of 13 RefSeq proteomes, comprising two dicot species (Arabidopsis thaliana and Solanum lycopersicum) and eleven monocot species (Zea mays, Triticum aestivum, Setaria viridis, Phragmites australis, Phoenix dactylifera, Oryza sativa, Musa acuminata, Lolium perenne, Hordeum vulgare subsp. vulgare, Brachypodium distachyon, and Asparagus officinalis) (Toghani and Kamoun, 2024).

Chapter 8/Materials and Methods

Declaration of Artificial Intelligence usage

1 min read

I used Claude (Anthropic) to assist in setting up the initial Git repository and LaTeX project structure, document templates, and syntax. I also consulted Claude to draft preliminary chapter outlines synthesized from my published manuscripts and PhD progress reports. Over the course of writing, these outlines and the structure of each chapter were substantially revised, expanded, and refined independently through my own work. This approach was discussed with my PhD supervisory committee and complies fully with the University of East Anglia policy on the use of artificial intelligence in research and thesis writing. A complete export of all interactive transcripts is openly archived in the accompanying Zenodo repository (Toghani, 2026).

Publications and datasets

During my PhD, I had the opportunity to participate in many projects and contribute to several publications and datasets. This appendix lists the publications and datasets resulting from this work. Under each entry, I provide a statement detailing my specific contribution to the project. Entries are arranged by year, with the most recent listed first.

(†) indicates joint first authorship. (*) indicates a corresponding author.

Papers and preprints

  1. Posbeyikian A.†, Toghani A.†, McClelland A.J.†, Kamoun S.*, Sugihara Y.*, Contreras M.P.* (2026) Fold on tight: ten things to know about AI structure prediction in plant immunity. Zenodo. doi:10.5281/zenodo.22100278

    Together with colleagues at TSL and ZMBP, I co-authored a review synthesizing recent developments in plant immunity into ten practical lessons for applying AI protein structure prediction across the plant sciences.

  2. Feng L.†, Hou Y.†, Toghani A., Wang Z., Tang B., Atkinson N., Li H., Qiao Y., Wang Y., Hua J., Zhai J., Ma W.* (2026) A conserved small RNA-generating gene cluster undergoes sequence diversification and contributes to plant immunity. Nature Communications. doi:10.1038/s41467-026-77164-1

  3. Pai H., Sakai T., Posbeyikian A., Frijters R., Sugihara Y., Contreras M.P., Kourelis J., Adachi H., Kamoun S.*, Toghani A.* (2026) Contrasting evolutionary patterns of helper and sensor NRC NLRs in lettuce reflect functional divergence following subfunctionalization. PLOS Genetics. doi:10.1371/journal.pgen.1012245

    This work forms the basis of Chapters 4 and 6 of this thesis. I led the project, performed the evolutionary and phylogenetic analyses of NLRs, drafted the manuscript, and prepared the figures.

  4. Gao C.†, Meng X.†, Chen X., Yang L., Ibrahim T., Toghani A., Yuen E.L.H., Eilmann N., King F., Li K., Wang L., Sun B., Wang Y., Bozkurt T.O.*, Dong S.* (2026) Surface immune signaling unlocks NLR activation through mRNA alternative splicing. Science. doi:10.1126/science.adx9929

  5. Madhuprakash J., Toghani A., Pai H., Harvey M., Bentham A.R., Seager B.A., Yuen E.L.H., De la Concepcion J.C., Lawson D.M., Stevenson C.E.M., Vergara-Cruces A., Derevnina L., Bozkurt T.O., Banfield M.J., Kamoun S.*, Contreras M.P.* (2026) An effector from the potato late blight pathogen bridges ENTH-domain protein TOL9a to an activated helper NLR to suppress immunity.   6. Toghani A.†, Garro M.†, Frijters R., Kamoun S.*, Contreras M.P.* (2026) A conserved structural logic underlies sensor–helper NLR communication in the NRC immune receptor network. bioRxiv. doi:10.64898/2026.05.18.725810

  7. Toghani A.†, Seager B.A.†, Sugihara Y., Roijen L.-M., Azcue J.M., Garro M., Sargolzaei M., Morianou I., Harant A., Gallop S., Kourelis J., MacLean D., Contreras M.P., Kamoun S.*, Lüdke D.* (2026) AI-guided discovery of atypical protein assemblies. bioRxiv. doi:10.64898/2026.05.03.722499

  8. Selvaraj M., Toghani A., Pai H., Sugihara Y., Kourelis J., Yuen E.L.H., Ibrahim T., Zhao H., Xie R., Maqbool A., De la Concepcion J.C., Banfield M.J., Derevnina L., Petre B., Lawson D.M., Bozkurt T.O., Wu C.-H., Kamoun S.*, Contreras M.P.* (2024) Activation of plant immunity through conversion of a helper NLR homodimer into a resistosome. Datasets

  1. Toghani A., Seager B.A., Lüdke D., Kamoun S. (2026) AlphaFold 3 hexameric resistosome models for 637 NRC-clade NLR proteins from Solanaceae. Zenodo. doi:10.5281/zenodo.19860917

  2. Toghani A., Sugihara Y., Kamoun S. (2026) Harmonized genome annotation of 346 Solanaceae species reveals 197,834 NLR immune receptors. Zenodo. doi:10.5281/zenodo.19855162

  3. Toghani A., Sugihara Y., Kamoun S. (2025) Deep-learning-based annotation of 230 superasterid genomes reveals a harmonized dataset of 91,366 NLRs. Dryad. doi:10.5061/dryad.sxksn03d6

  4. Toghani A., Kamoun S. (2024) Functional annotation of 180 RefSeq reference plant proteomes reveals a dataset of 113,684 NLR proteins. Zenodo. zenodo.org/records/13627395

  5. Toghani A., Bozkurt T.O., Kamoun S. (2024) AlphaFold 3 predicted NLR resistosome structures. Zenodo. doi:10.5281/zenodo.11546021

  6. Sugihara Y., Toghani A., Kamoun S., Kourelis J. (2023) NLRome dataset from 124 genomes of plants in the Solanaceae family. Zenodo. doi:10.5281/zenodo.10354349

Acknowledgments

I would like to start by thanking my supervisor, Sophien, for his continued support and encouragement. Throughout my time at TSL, you always provided a sea of ideas and were never shy about discussing science with me, even if it meant me dropping by your office literally every day. Thank you for being the best mentor I could have ask for and for nurturing an environment that allowed me to do my research with the utmost joy. I would also like to thank my secondary supervisor, Phil Carella. Thank you, Phil, for your insights and support before and during my PhD. My sincere thanks also go to my undergraduate supervisors and mentors, Professors Nematollah Etemadi, Mahdi Gheysari, Aghafakhr Mirlohi, and Rahim Mehrabi. Without your encouragement and guidance, I could not have reached this point. I also want to thank Sebastian Schornak for his support and career advice over the years.

Being part of the “Kamounity” has been a delightful experience and a true privilege. Throughout the years, I worked with many talented colleagues and friends whom I learned so much from; each of you shaped my PhD and predoc journey. Thank you to everyone who makes this place so magical.
